#3652. Carrie Coon on ‘The Gilded Age’, ‘The Liberation’, and Parenting

Carrie Coon and I are supposed to be talking about her new film, The Liberation—a gripping drama about a suburban mother who leaves her family to join an all-woman cult in the 1980s. But when we meet for tea at the London West Hollywood hotel, it doesn’t take long for our conversation to turn to general doom and gloom. Between the moment I order a custom-made ginger tea—which I’m now calling “the Carrie Coon special”—and when it arrives at our table, we’ve already started talking about fascism in America, how hard it is for an actor to find enough work to earn health insurance, global warming, and the devastating fires in Los Angeles.

“I don’t do small talk anymore. I’m not good at it,” says Coon, taking a sip from her own ginger tea—a blend she started having this restaurant make for her after getting hooked on it while filming The White Lotus in Thailand. “I’m just like, ‘So we’re all going to die. How you feeling about that?’”

But even when she’s talking fire and brimstone, Coon’s charming warmth keeps the conversation from being too dark and stormy. If Coon were leading a cult, I might join. She’s funny and empathetic; she makes this sweet, quick “aww” sound if you compliment her or share something she’s sympathetic with. Maybe Coon, who was raised in Ohio, simply can’t shed her Midwestern sensibility, even though she transforms onscreen into characters with much harder, and sometimes pricklier, outer shells. Coon has earned four Emmy nominations for playing the stubborn small-town cop Gloria Burgle in Fargo, the lonely lawyer Laurie Duffy in The White Lotus, and twice for the ambitious social climber Bertha Russell on The Gilded Age, which just debuted its fourth season on HBO.

Carrie Coon and Morgan Spector in season 2 of The Gilded Age.

She reveals a different side of herself in The Liberation, Guy Nattiv’s drama that opens in limited (and Oscar-qualifying) release November 6 before going wide January 8. Her character, Rita Cooper, is a Holocaust survivor whose trauma and stagnation in her family life cause her to abandon her husband (Tracy Letts, Coon’s real-life husband) and two daughters (Bella Ramsey and Odessa Young) for an all-female spiritual group led by a charismatic leader named Ricki (Lily James).

The film is a strong showcase for Coon as she transforms both physically and emotionally. When Rita joins the commune, she loses weight and her identity as she falls further under Ricki’s spell. “People are struck by me playing someone who feels weaker or more frail, because I’m often put into roles where I’m strong, verbal, intellectual, brassy,” says Coon. “I think it’s unusual for them to see that level of vulnerability in my performances. But of course, I think of myself as capable of all that.”

I nervously admit to Coon that when I watched The Liberation, I was troubled to find that, as a mother of two young kids, I could understand Rita’s choice—to leave behind all the demands and burdens of family and household, to run to a place where you could focus solely on yourself. It’s hard to say this out loud.

Coon makes that sympathetic “aww” sound. “We all have that moment. It’s a fantasy, but haven’t we all thought, ‘I could leave right now; what would happen if I just didn’t come back?’” she says. “That’s why I found her so compelling, because she walked away from her family and chose to invest in her self-actualization and her healing in the ’80s. It’s a really risky choice, but, I suppose, just undeniable for her.”

Coon and Letts, who married in 2013—in a hospital where Letts had just received emergency gallbladder surgery—have two kids together who are now five and eight years old, just a few years ahead of my own. Juggling life as a working mother can be challenging, especially in invisible ways. “I think a lot of the cognitive load is so heavy, and people don’t really understand,” says Coon.

Carrie Coon, Leslie Bibb, and Michelle Monaghan in The White Lotus.

When Coon was cast in the third season of HBO’s hit The White Lotus, playing a woman who goes on a luxury vacation with her two longtime best friends, she was gone for a total of 10 weeks. At the time, her daughter was only three. “That was very hard, and that was a very difficult decision,” she says. “I’m not sure it was a great decision, ultimately. I don’t know if we would do it again the same way.”

She’s had other moments of feeling spread too thin, especially just before she went to film His Three Daughters—the 2023 movie that cast Coon, Natasha Lyonne, and Elizabeth Olsen as three sisters who reunite to care for their ailing father. “I turned to Tracy and said, ‘I can’t do this anymore. I can’t do both things,’” she remembers. Maybe as her kids get older— “little kids, little problems, big kids, big problems,” she says—she will actually have to shift her focus. “In this world where we have no schema to navigate the challenges they’re facing, I would have to take a step back again and be with them,” she says. “I don’t know. It’s hard to say.”

Elizabeth Olsen and Carrie Coon in His Three Daughters.

Coon and Letts’s kids joined them for part of the time while they filmed The Liberation in Vancouver. During the first half of the movie, Coon wore hip pads and other body-shaping additions to make Rita seem more weighed down by her responsibility and the trauma of having been a child in a concentration camp. Coon says she could also lean into the exhaustion she already felt: “We were co-sleeping in a little apartment, and it was not easy,” she says. “And so I was like, ‘Great, I don’t have to look like anything. I could just be tired.’ So I kind of allowed that exhaustion I normally feel, which I try to overcome in my daily life, just to creep in more.”

When Rita leaves her family for the isolated commune, Coon’s environment also shifted: She moved to a new filming location, and her family left town. In the mornings, she’d swim or stretch. She’d also lost 10 pounds and shorn her hair for the role, transforming from Rita into Naya—the new name Ricki gives her character, a common practice in cults. “Carrie’s a very, very strong, physical actress,” says Nattiv. “Rita is the matriarch of her family. She’s a strong woman, intelligent—and then she’s not. She loses everything. It was amazing to see how she shifts between Naya and Rita.”

Nattiv based The Liberation on his grandmother Rita—who really had been in a concentration camp as a child, and joined a commune in her adult life. Rita had given testimony to Yad Vashem, the World Holocaust Remembrance Center; Coon watched it as she prepared to play the role. She also watched and listened to hours of testimonies of women who had been in concentration camps in Poland, learning “the sort of very specific way that particular trauma is held in the body, the challenge of speaking the unspeakable.”

I wondered if watching so many hours of these stories, so much horror and pain, was difficult. “Well, if I’m really honest, I found that I was drawn to listening to them instead of the news,” says Coon. “I started listening to them as a comfort, because they were a story of resilience. Thinking about the unspeakable atrocities that were happening around me in my very own country with my own tax dollars—and yet here are people on the other side of something like that, articulating those stories and what they learned.”

The present political climate is ever-present in Coon’s mind, as well as on her social media accounts. (A few of her more recent X posts: “Failed president,” “Close the camps,” “The president has nothing but ‘tranny’ jokes. How pathetic. How empty.”) For the past few weeks, she’s been encouraging people to vote, especially her fellow Ohioans. As she admitted, she’s not one for small talk.

Carrie Coon (center) with Odessa Young, Bella Ramsey, Sharon Taylor, and Tracy Letts in The Liberation.

“It’s absurd. It’s untenable,” she says. “We’re in a really precarious moment because people’s lives are untenable all across the board.” She recognizes her own privilege—that she and her husband are both able to work, that they can afford childcare—but says she’s worried for actors who can’t find roles in this shrinking economy. “Even just the labor of making tapes, the free labor, there’s no protection,” she says. “We have these rules in our union, but no one’s really following those rules. What young actor is going to make that phone call and complain?”

She’s also noticing how few female-centered films get told on the biggest stages, with the biggest budgets. “What happens when you’re living in an authoritarian regime is everybody gets scared, and everybody gets safe, and everyone’s making really safe choices. It’s not what people want,” she says. “Women are tremendous economic drivers in this economy, and we still aren’t making art for them.”

Coon will do her part, with films like The Liberation. She’s wrapped work on another independent movie, Honeymoon/Funeral, a romantic comedy from Fresh Off the Boat creator Nahnatchka Khan that also stars Rebecca Ferguson and Greta Lee. Next year, Letts heads to London from April through October to do Death of a Salesman at The National, which means more maneuvering for their family unit. “We’re thrilled for him. And yet that’s going to be a really interesting time for our family,” she says. “So I don’t have as much work lined up, and I’m okay to be patient. I feel good about being patient right now.”

But she does have one wish for the future: She’d like to do a comedy. “No one’s letting me do that. My family is surprised by my career because it’s just not the way I occurred to them as a person at all. People are expecting to meet a very serious and lugubrious actress that needs a lot of special drinks or something,” she says. While taking another sip from her custom, off-menu ginger tea.

Shortly after its debut, Lena Dunham's Girls joined the ranks of HBO shows that got the world talking. The Golden Globe-winning comedy (which is streaming with a HBO Max subscription) was a snapshot for millennials in their 20s, and has had a resurgence in recent years. A few weeks ago Dunham announced that she show was returning for a five-episode limited revival, and fans like me have been wondering if Adam Driver would be back as his character Adam Sackler. So when CinemaBlend sat down for an interview with the Oscar-nominated actor, we had to ask him.

When Lena Dunham made the announcement of Girls returning, it came with confirmation that we'll also see Allison Williams' Marnie, Jemima Kirke's Jessa, Zosia Mamet's Shoshana and Andrew Rannells' Elijah. Still, fans wondered if Adam would also be back. CinemaBlend spoke with Driver about his new movie Paper Tiger, where we asked if he should expect him to reprise his role. He told us:

There you have it. While the jury is still out on a number of the other boys from Girls, fans shouldn't expect to see Adam Driver's character to appear in the limited revival. This is a bummer for sure, and now I'm curious to see how the character of Adam will be addressed when the show returns. After all, he had a long romantic history with both Hannah and Jessa by the time the original show ended. You can see Driver's comments for yourself below:

A post shared by CinemaBlend (@cinemablend)

Those who have been closely following discourse surrounding Girls might not be all that surprised by the Star Wars actor's response. Over the summer Lena Dunham made some allegations about working with Driver in her new memoir Famesick. She detailed their unique working relationship, and specific confrontations like Driver allegedly throwing a chair and being "verbally aggressive" in her trailer. For his part, the 42 year-old actor hasn't weighed in much on the drama. Instead he claimed that his perspective will be shared later as he was "saving it all for my book".

While promoting her book, Lena Dunham spoke about being surprised by the audience's reaction to Adam on Girls. The character had a pretty wild arc throughout the show's six seasons on the air, ping ponging between being a romantic lead and volatile and strange character. When we last saw him he was still dating Jemima Kirke's Jessa, with that romantic relationship greatly altering her friendship with Dunham's protagonist Hannah.

Lena Dunham has joked about what various Girls characters might be up to nowadays, and now fans will get to actually see them return when the show airs five new episodes. Unfortunately we won't see more from Adam, but hopefully we get some references to what he's up to anyway. For now fans will have to wait for news about other boys from the show like Alexander Karpovsky's Ray and Ebon Moss-Bachrach's Desi.

Girls is streaming in its entirety over on HBO Max. The revival isn't on the 2026 TV schedule, so we'll have to be patient while waiting to reunite with the beloved characters of Dunham's comedy series.

#3650. Inside PS, The Private Members-Only Terminals at LAX, Miami, and Paris Airports

There are 10 terminals at the Los Angeles International Airport. One through nine are for the general public: terminal one for Southwest, terminal two for Virgin Atlantic, the international hub in the numberless terminal B. Each one is packed with weary, edgy travelers lined up for security, coffee, or a meal. You arrive at your terminal via rideshare and depart via rideshare—so long as your ride is a premium black car. If it isn’t, you must take a 20-minute bus ride to a parking lot called “LAX-it,” where you wait amongst the hordes for your UberX to arrive as it slowly inches through crippling traffic.

The 10th terminal promises to deliver you from this misery. It’s around the back of the airport complex, off the 105 in El Segundo, next to several cargo holds and a Gate Gourmet facility where airplane meals are carted off to various jets on the tarmac. When you arrive, no one asks for a boarding pass. A security guard checks your name off a list, and a valet whisks away your bags with care before you’re ushered into your own private suite with amenities galore: squishy velvet couches and boucle chairs, Assouline coffee table books, free iPhone chargers, and chocolate-covered almonds and gummy bears. A fridge comes with sparkling waters and canned matcha drinks—a far cry from the plastic Dasani bottles found at Hudson News. A private bathroom boasts Le Labo soaps.

While you’re waiting for your flight, you can get a manicure, a table massage, or even a haircut. You can request a pair of Normatec Elite compression boots (retail price: $1,099) to help with your circulation before takeoff. Or if you are feeling more social, you can head to “the Salon,” where abstract art hangs on the wall and chandeliers dangle from the ceiling. Order the coconut chia pudding or bagel-and-lox platter if you’re there for breakfast, duck confit agnolotti or a Mediterranean chicken panini on house-made ciabatta for lunch. For dinner, there’s a New York strip, and caviar service is always available.

When it’s time to go, you’ll pass through a private security check with a dedicated TSA agent. Then you’ll climb in a BMW (suitcases already loaded) which drives you across the tarmac directly to your plane. Forget boarding with Zone 8 or gatechecking your carry-on.

The Salon at PS at LAX, designed by Elle Decor A-List interior designer Cliff Fong.

This is PS at LAX—a private, members only terminal at Los Angeles International. It’ll cost you to get in: One-time access to the Salon (and nothing else) without a membership is priced at $1,295. For frequent fliers, an annual baseline membership starts at $1,250 and goes up to $4,850. Private suites cost an additional $3,650 or $4,950 for four people, depending on the type of membership.

Unsurprisingly, it’s become a see-and-don’t-be-seen hub for LA celebrities wary of attracting the camera-wielding masses at commercial airports (and the paparazzi that stake out the terminal). Gigi Hadid, Gabrielle Union, Hailey Bieber, Jamie Foxx, and Kourtney Kardashian are just some of the famous faces that are known to frequent PS at LAX.

But this year, PS is pushing beyond the Hollywood stars eager to escape the clutches of Deuxmoi. In the past six months, the firm has opened private terminals in Miami (taking over the historic Pan-Am space) and Dallas. Paris is coming in early 2027. The seclusion, the gourmet food, and the luxurious interiors (curated by Elle Decor A-List designers Jean Liu for Dallas and Cliff Fong for Miami and LA) are all nice draws, but there's another reason PS CEO Amina Belouizdad Porter cites for why customers are willing to shell out thousands of dollars on top of a first-class ticket.

The Atlanta airport on March 23, 2026. Government shutdowns have caused disastrous scenes at American commercial terminals.

Because, well, it has been. The last fiscal year has seen three government shutdowns, the longest of which lasted for 76 days. TSA Deputy Administrator Ha Nguyen McNeill told Congress that the agency experienced the longest security wait times in its 24-year history during the shutdown that stretched from February 14 to April 30, 2026. Some airports, including Atlanta, had lines up to five hours long. The logistical meltdowns hit at a time when air travel has never been more popular: In 2025, nearly 907 million people flew commercially in the United States. Belouizdad Porter says that those disruptions led to a direct increase in PS customers.

The growing crowds at airport lounges also nudged some travelers over the edge. Credit card companies long ago realized that offering lounge access enticed new customers, with Chase, American Express, Citi, Capital One, and more getting in the game. But demand exceeded square footage, and many of those lounges suffered from overcrowding and subpar service, selling the dream of an aero oasis that never was.

“There have never been more airport lounges,” David Mack writes in the New York Times, “Yet there also have never seemed to be more lounges that are not worth the hassle…Sometimes the lines for the lounges are the longest in the airport.”

(Though the only thing worse than an overcrowded airport lounge might be getting stranded outside. Reddit is currently up in arms about the obscene food prices at the newly renovated Burbank Airport in California—price tag: $1.3 billion—where a cheese and bean burrito costs $25.)

Another contributing factor? The rising costs of private jets. While the terms “one percent” or “.1 percent” are often thrown around when it comes to PJ owners, the reality is only 0.003 percent of America’s population can afford even fractional ownership. Demand for private aircraft surged after the pandemic, raising prices, and now the average net worth of those who own a jet is $190 million. For those with fractional ownership, it’s $140 million. Yet there are still plenty of mere decamillionaires looking to dodge the misery of the airport. As Sartre put it: Hell is other people.

Previously, “You could either fly round-trip first class for $6,000 but deal with the airport, the friction, and the crowd,” Belouizdad Porter says. “Or you could fly private round-trip and it's $200,000.” PS operates somewhere in between. “I think there’s a real appetite for that middle ground: the convenience of private aviation without the commitment or expense of chartering an entire plane,” says Lucie Kittel, founder of luxury travel advisory firm Domino Travel.

And besides, even if you do reach the level of private jet ownership, you still can’t always avoid the flying masses. A midsize jet that fits six to nine people costs between $10 and $20 million dollars and can fly 2,000 to 3,000 nautical miles. If it’s on the shorter end of that range, it can just make a trip from New York to California—but not to Europe. There’s also the issue of safety: The country is currently facing a pilot shortage, and more experienced candidates often work with mainstream airlines who can provide higher salaries. Larger planes can also better navigate rough weather.

Carriers like United and Delta know all of this, which is why they’re beefing up their luxury experiences. Delta recently announced it was investing over $1 billion in retrofitting its premium cabins, and new Delta One Terminals at JFK and LAX allow first-class ticket holders to avoid overcrowded TSA lines and the standard lounge. “Most of my clients flying out of JFK are choosing Delta One,” Kittel adds, “and they love the experience.”

Thanks to the artificial intelligence boom—the latest phase of a 15-year bull market for stocks—there’s been an explosion of multi-multi-millionaires in America. While not all of them can fly private, they certainly can devote large sums of money to separating themselves from the hoi polloi. Both startups like PS and established players are now competing for that sub-ultra-wealthy dollar.

#3649. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

Dwayne Johnson is typically down for anything when he hosts Saturday Night Live. Michael Che singled out the A-Lister and former WWE Champion in a recent interview as one of his favorite hosts specifically because he always shows up open to any ideas. You can really see that across his five hosting appearances too. The writers clearly go harder and pitch weirder concepts for him than many other hosts because he’s down to try whatever like say The Rock Obama. That doesn’t mean, however, that there’s not the occasional idea he’ll still veto.

During that aforementioned conversation with Complex, the longtime Weekend Update co-anchor said he once pitched The Rock an absolutely filthy sketch that didn’t happen. The actor was promoting his initial casting as Black Adam; so, Che pitched another kind of Black Adam sketch that would see The Rock playing Adam from Adam and Eve. Instead of having his rib removed to make Eve, however, Adam was apparently going to tell God it was because he wanted to go down on himself. Here’s a portion of his quote…

I had one for the Rock that he didn’t do, but it was during Black Adam and he was playing Adam from Adam and Eve,and he asked God to remove his ribs so he could go down on himself.

I have no idea why Johnson turned the sketch down. Maybe it was because it’s blasphemous. Maybe it’s because it has the potential to be racially problematic. Maybe it’s because he didn’t want to wear the fig leaf or whatever the costume would have required. Maybe it just didn’t speak to him. Regardless, it’s interesting that Che told the story but then also specifically mentioned that The Rock, at least compared to other hosts was down for almost anything.

I feel like The Rock was the best. He was down for everything. He’s like legit funny, consummate professional, could do anything.

This conversation really makes me wonder how many hosts are just turning down things left and right. There are always stories going around about certain hosts being difficult to work with or saying no to anything that might be even the slightest bit problematic, but maybe the average host coming in is giving a lot more nos than we realize too. That would explain why Johnson is getting his shine here in the middle of a story about him passing on a sketch.

Regardless, it’s clearly all love between Johnson and everyone at SNL. He liked the Instagram post with this video, and he’s also spoken very highly of the show in interviews. He’s even be willing to come back for cameos when he’s not the full blown host, obviously because he enjoys the process and being around all the people.

Unfortunately it’s now been almost ten years since Johnson last hosted SNL. He’s obviously been very busy crushing it as one of the biggest stars in Hollywood during that lost decade, but I’m really hoping he’ll find some time in his schedule to return and host again. As Che said, he’s up for (almost) anything, and pairing that willingness with his natural charisma and fantastic comedic timing is always a recipe for a good episode.

Even without The Rock, SNL should give us a fantastic stretch of episodes coming up thanks to some compelling upcoming hosts. Druski is set to take the reigns this weekend, and he’ll be followed by John Mulaney, both of whom should give us plenty of standout moments.

#3647. Critical Role Officially Returns to Its Roots for New Campaign with Hololive

All the details about Shattered Legends, the new Critical Role x Hololive Daggerheart series

Announced in October, Shattered Legends is an upcoming miniseries featuring Critical Role and members of Hololive Production. Critical Role founders Matt Mercer and Marisha Ray will team up with Hololive’s Nerissa Ravencroft, Mori Calliope, Shiori Novella, and Gigi Murin​​​​ for a new adventure set in the world of Exandria, where the Critical Role story began with Campaign 1: Vox Machina.

Shattered Legends will premiere on Nov. 13 at 6 p.m. PT / 9 p.m. ET on Nerissa Ravencroft's YouTube channel and on Critical Role's streaming platform, Beacon. The six-episode actual play show will use the rules for Daggerheart, the tabletop role-playing game designed by Critical Role's publishing studio, Darrington Press. Mercer will take the role of Game Master, while Ray will sit on the players' side of the table along with the Hololive crew, helping them navigate a treacherous new adventure in Exandria.

Shattered Legends is set in the Shattered Teeth archipelago, located southeast of Tal'dorei, the continent where the first Critical Role campaign, Vox Machina, takes place. The adventurers will explore the island of Ubradar, and more specifically a mysterious location known as the Undermaw, "a massive sinkhole with an unknown darkness sealed below," according to a news release. If this reminds you of the popular anime Made in Abyss, the similarities don't end there. In the Shattered Teeth islands, time flows differently than in the outside world, just like in Made in Abyss' eponymous giant hole in the ground.

The characters and classes for each of the players in Shattered Legends have also been revealed. Marisha Ray plays tidekin witch Florence, "a moon witch of the sea who believes she guides the souls of lost sailors to the afterlife of the Sister Divas." Nerissa Ravencroft plays elf rogue Siliul 'Sil' Faeli, "a noble turned rogue and skilled tracker seeking refuge on Ubradar." Mori Calliope plays infernis bard Kaz Oogod, "the last of the Oogod clan, a young musician with a 'world-changing instrument.'" Shiori Novella plays fungrin druid Marchen 'March' Rosemyne, "an orphan searching for the Huntsman she lives with, aided by her connection to nature and a network of mushrooms." Finally, Gigi Murin plays faerie seraph Giryn, "a devoted follower of Mother Liopé on a mission to spread the Enclave’s teachings and witness the nature of life and death."

The Hololive cast members will appear with new virtual avatars based on the spectacular design of their characters, as seen in the presentation video below. Mercer and Ray will appear in the flesh, even if many fans are complaining this was a missed opportunity to give them a virtual avatar.

Shattered Legends will not end with the six-episode miniseries. A promotional tour will hit conventions in North America, Europe, and Asia, starting with a panel at Anime Frontier in Fort Worth, Texas, on Dec. 5.

If you miss Tal'dorei and the setting of the adventures of Vox Machina, or if you're just curious to see how a group of cheery VTubers will react to Mercer's evil Game Master shenanigans, tune in to Shattered Legends when it premieres on Nov. 13.

#3646. Susie Wiles Is Out. What Will Trump Do When He Runs Out of Women to Fire?

You know how after millions of people make clear that they despise not just your political project but also you personally, the logical response is to triple down on the specific things they hate?

That’s Donald Trump’s signature move. Three days after Democrats flipped seven Senate seats—nine if you feel bullish on Mississippi and Alaska—and secured a House majority, winning 253 seats and counting, the president announced that his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, would be replaced by Stephen Miller.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Even though polls indicating a blue wave proliferated before the election, this particular outcome still comes as a surprise. After all, Wiles had apparently proven her ability to ride out storms before—including everything that rocked Trump’s 2024 campaign, which Wiles managed, and her choice to sit for 10 interviews with Vanity Fair’s Chris Whipple in 2025, during which she discussed Elon Musk’s drug use and JD Vance’s true motives for embracing Trump. “Despite his travails, Trump needs Wiles and almost everyone around him knows it,” Whipple recently wrote in a follow-up story tracing rumors of Wiles’s imminent axing.

But now Wiles’s luck has finally run out. Why? Perhaps because she is, in the end, a woman.

Trump’s first term was marked by all sorts of chaos, including frequent arrivals to and departures from the White House. (Remember Omarosa?) But it doesn’t take Jessica Fletcher to detect that this time around, there’s a distinct pattern when it comes to whom Trump is willing to toss aside when the going gets rough. The scalps of the no-scalps era all have barrel curls. As Texas representative Jasmine Crockett observed in April, “He will throw the incompetent women under the bus a lot faster than the incompetent men.”

On March 5, following an uprising against the administration’s mass-deportation effort that culminated in two protesters being killed by ICE agents in Minnesota, Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem was axed. After wrath over the administration’s botched handling of the Epstein files, Attorney General Pam Bondi was fired in April.

Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Trump’s labor secretary, resigned later that month amid a misconduct investigation. Tulsi Gabbard, the director of national intelligence, who couldn’t sell Trump’s disastrous war with Iran, submitted her resignation in May, after her husband was diagnosed with cancer. Press secretary Karoline Leavitt stepped down—of her own accord—in August. Following an embarrassing Wall Street Journal investigation, Kimberly Guilfoyle, the ambassador to Greece—and former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr.—was forced to resign last month.

Though you may have already forgotten all about her, Katie Zacharia had perhaps the least distinguished tenure of all: She gave her first briefing as Trump’s new press secretary on a Tuesday and was forced out by Friday of the same week. Shortly before Wiles’s ouster this week, Harmeet Dhillon, who helped kill DEI after joining the civil rights division of Trump’s Justice Department, announced she was stepping down.

All this, and Pete Hegseth still has a job.

What are we to make of the fact that Trump’s departed all happen to harbor two X chromosomes? Could it be, perhaps, that President “Grab ’Em by the Pussy” has a problem with women—even the loyalists who are largely responsible for helping him claw his way back into the White House in the first place? (Does Trump win, or even run, in 2024 without Wiles? It’s a possibility I’d like to see Rodham author Curtis Sittenfeld explore in an upcoming novel.)

The one thing we can be sure about is that, as of right now, there are only three women left in Trump’s 21-person Cabinet. The members of that trio—Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Education Secretary Linda McMahon, and Kelly Loeffler, administrator of the Small Business Administration—might want to watch their blowout. (So should Natalie Harp.) Perhaps after they go, Trump will start employing the principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion while stabbing his allies in the back.

#3645. The JBL Vibe Beam Earbuds Are on Sale for $30 Right Now

If you want reliable earbuds that cost less than tonight's dinner, JBL is a reliable brand to fall back on, with plenty of budget-friendly models that lack the bells and whistles of pricier options while still delivering on sound and battery life. One of the most popular picks is the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds, which are down 40% at $29.99 (originally $49.95).

These earbuds aren’t reinventing the wheel, but they do check important boxes. They last up to eight hours without the charging case, and up to 32 hours with the case. Ten minutes of charging will get you a couple of hours of playback, and they have an IP54 rating, making them dust- and splash-resistant. The built-in mics work well in reasonably quiet rooms, but may struggle to separate your voice from loud background noise. Another perk is Find My Buds, which helps locate misplaced earbuds via a sound that’s played.

With 8 mm dynamic drivers, they deliver punchy bass that translates well to adrenaline-pumping workout music, and adequate vocal clarity for music and podcasts. Though the default tuning is relatively balanced, you can tweak it on the app’s equalizer to adjust it to your liking. They lack ANC and Bluetooth multipoint pairing, which isn’t surprising given the price point, but still pack in a solid amount of features and quality into $30, making the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds a good value for everyday bargain earbuds that get the job done.

Sir Patrick Stewart’s death hit a lot of people hard, from his fans to his co-stars. The tributes for the late Marvel actor have been incredibly touching, too. One co-star, Dafne Keen, who appeared alongside Stewart in her first film, Logan, as Laura/X-23, recently appeared on the podcast Inside of You with Michael Rosenbaum. It’s such a lovely sentiment that has been once again mourning the death of the MCU and Star Trek star.

During their long discussion, the subject of filming the movie and working alongside Stewart and Hugh Jackman came up. Keen praised both actors for the way they treated her on set, saying they were not only incredibly professional, but they took the young actress (Keen was 11 years old when production began) under their wing and really looked out for her. She talked about dancing on set with Jackman (everyone’s dream, right?) and how much everyone in the cast meant to her.

When Rosenbaum asked her about Stewart, she opened up about how great he was on set:

Oh, he's incredible. He's such a wise professional. He's such a professional, but he's also, which I think not a lot of people know, he's hilarious. He is so charming and so hilarious. And he was so nurturing and warm to me, and he's so good with children. He was so amazing.

I’ll be honest, I tried to figure out when this interview was recorded and couldn’t (it was released on November 3rd), but it was recorded before the X-Men star died on October 28, it seems. As it was recorded before the world found out the devastating news, it only serves to show just how beloved Patrick Stewart was to everyone he came in contact with. His death and the tributes after it are right in line with what people thought before it, like Keen.

From Star Trek co-stars to those who love the MCU to everyone else who worked with Stewart on other projects, there is literally no one who has anything but absolute praise for the late actor. He died last week at age 86 after a brief battle with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia.

Stewart is set to posthumously appear in the upcoming MCU film Avengers: Doomsday, reprising the role he played so often in his life, including alongside Keen and Jackman in Logan. This may very well be his final appearance as Professor X, though we don’t know a lot of details about the follow-up to Doomsday, Avengers: Secret Wars, which will hit the 2027 movie schedule a year from December.

It’s quite the legacy, one that lives on in the memories of his fans and co-workers, of which Keen is both.

#3643. SCOTUS sets hearing date for Apple’s appeal in Epic Games case

The U.S. Supreme Court has officially scheduled oral arguments in Apple’s appeal in its long-running legal battle with Epic Games. Here are the details.

Back in 2020, Epic Games sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store for introducing an alternative in-app payment system through a remotely activated update.

The following year, despite ruling in Apple’s favor on nine of Epic’s ten claims, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled that Apple could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment options outside the App Store.

As a result, Apple changed its rules to allow external purchase links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on transactions completed through them, along with restrictions on how those links could be presented.

Epic challenged Apple’s implementation, and the district court agreed. In April 2025, Judge Rogers ordered Apple to remove those restrictions and stop charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store, finding the company in civil contempt for violating the original injunction.

Since then, Apple has allowed developers to direct users to external payment options in the US App Store without charging a commission, while continuing to challenge the contempt ruling.

After unsuccessful attempts before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, Apple eventually took its case to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to review whether Apple could be held in contempt for violating the “spirit” of an injunction, even when its text did not specifically prohibit the conduct in question.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only review the civil contempt ruling, not how much, if anything, Apple can charge developers for purchases made outside the App Store. That issue is being handled separately by the district court, after the Ninth Circuit overturned the blanket ban on commissions in December.

Earlier today, the Supreme Court’s official docket for the case was updated with a date for oral arguments.

According to the filing, Apple and Epic Games will present their arguments before the Supreme Court on Monday, January 11, 2027, though both sides have already outlined many of their arguments in recent filings.

In September, Apple filed its opening brief with the Supreme Court, arguing that the contempt ruling should be overturned because the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit it from charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store.

In its brief, Apple cited multiple court decisions to support its argument that a party cannot be held in civil contempt unless an injunction clearly prohibits the conduct in question.

A few days after Apple’s filing, the US Department of Justice and several legal and business groups also submitted briefs supporting at least part of the company’s argument.

The DOJ, however, also argued that the lower courts were right to hold Apple in contempt over some of its restrictions on external purchase links, including a requirement that developers use what Apple called “plain buttons,” which could not have contrasting backgrounds.

With the hearing now scheduled, the case is one step closer to a final decision from the Supreme Court. However, both sides still have some paperwork to submit before then, as Epic Games has until November 13 to file its brief responding to Apple’s arguments, while Apple’s reply is due December 14.

#3642. How the ‘Glee’ and ‘Girls’ Revivals Can Avoid Mistakes Made by Other TV Reboots

The blue-tinged afterglow of the 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both the House and Senate, unleashed a burst of online millennial optimism. Some have credited a pair of newly revived Obama-era coming of age TV shows that often got political themselves, Ryan Murphy’s Glee and Lena Dunham’s Girls, with being a precursor to the Blue Wave.

But for all of the internet’s excitement for new episodes of Glee and Girls , no one said aging beloved characters (who is Hannah Horvath at 40?), or addressing the current sociopolitical moment (will Sue Sylvester in a MAGA hat be inevitable?!) would come without risk. How do the Girls and Glee reboots meet nostalgic expectations while delivering something new and prescient about where the world is now? Perhaps Dunham and Murphy can draw lessons about aging gracefully in adaptation from revivals that have aired before them.

Ahead, a guide to do’s and don’ts for the return of generational TV, from the second coming of Sex and the City to Roseanne’s rocky renewal.

Riding a high from his Emmy-nominated shows including Ted Lasso and Shrinking (Apple TV), plus Rooster (HBO), series creator Bill Lawrence relaunched Scrubs, now airing its second season on ABC, into a post-Abbott Elementary landscape—where network TV craves workplace comedies for its airwaves. It seems that the folks behind Glee and Girls, respectively, have found the right moment to return to TV. Murphy has spoken about Glee’s recent streaming resurgence for younger audiences, and Dunham is coming off a headline-making book tour for her bestselling memoir Famesick, written about her time making Girls 1.0.

Rather than write themselves out of the show’s controversial final season, in which most of the show’s central cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, Sarah Chalke, were sidelined in favor of an entirely new group of characters, the creative team opted to retcon the entire ninth season and start fresh for the reboot. That means Glee can freely pretend its own flashforward—in which Rachel Berry is a surrogate mother for fellow Glee Club pals Kurt and Blaine could be abandoned. And maybe Shoshanna never decided she was too good for the rest of the Girls and they can all be dysfunctional friends again…right?

A political sketch titled “Oh Honey,” which reunited original cast members Debra Messing, Eric McCormack, Sean Hayes, and Megan Mullally in support of Hillary Clinton ahead of the 2016 presidential election, may not have prevented a Donald Trump presidency. But it did garner millions of views online, earning the attention of top NBC brass who hoped to capitalize on the nostalgia by relaunching Will & Grace in 2017. While the Glee Club has yet to release their own teaser, Dunham announced the Girls revival via four-way video call with cast members Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, and Zosia Mamet that promptly sent the internet into a tailspin.

While the Will & Grace revival lasted for three seasons largely because of its ability to engage with the day’s political issues, particularly as they related to the LGBTQ+ community, some felt the show became too steeped in Trumpland. In one episode, a Trump-supporting Karen even gets staunchly liberal Grace a job decorating his Oval Office. Girls and Glee will have to strike a similarly delicate balance with their own returns—incorporating the current political landscape in ways that feel natural to the narrative, as much as one can when often tone-deaf show choir kids and Brooklyn hipsters are involved.

Just as And Just Like That made a splash by murdering Mr. Big in the first episode via Peloton-induced heart attack, Glee and Girls should aim for maximum impact upon arrival. Maybe Adam Driver’s character meets his end while going method for a role and learning a dangerous new skill. As for Glee, perhaps the character played by Grammy-winning Finneas O’Connell (brother and music producer of Billie Eilish), could go up in a blaze of glory. Despite getting his start with a four-episode arc in the show’s final season, in 2020 O’Connell claimed that he’d never seen Glee, including the episodes he was in.

Taking a show outside of its comfort zone in the right ways raises the stakes—and highlights core tensions from the original series (see also: Miranda shown riding the subway for the first time). But some viewers felt And Just Like That… showrunner Michael Patrick King’s inclusion of diverse voices into the narrative veered too far outside of the shoebox with Che Diaz, the divisive podcast-cohost–slash-comedian–slash–veterinarian-office-worker that took the brunt of audience ire over freshly sober Miranda’s decision to divorce her husband Steve. New characters can become de facto villains for a series revival, particularly if they interfere with cherished dynamics from the show’s first run.

The return of Kelsey Grammer’s sitcom hero Frasier Crane was undercut by the absence of breakout supporting characters Niles and Daphne, as actors David Hyde Pierce and Jane Leeves did not reprise their roles for the reboot. Luckily, the core four of Girls have already signed on for their five-episode revival, and several Glee alums are in talks for its reboot, including series lead Lea Michele.

In addition to some of the creative challenges facing Frasier 2.0, the former NBC sitcom was welcomed back on Paramount+, a lesser-known streaming platform in comparison to Netflix or Peacock. At least it wasn’t Helen Hunt and Paul Reiser’s Mad About You, another ’90s NBC comedy that got its grand return on…Spectrum (?!) in 2019. Girls will air on HBO’s streaming partner, Max, and Glee is in the works via Disney+ and Hulu—barring any major industry mergers.

The Roseanne reboot earned new resonance in the zeitgeist—and major ratings on ABC—for its authentic depiction of a working-class Middle America family under Trump’s first presidency. Like the original 1988 series, the revival focused on the economic and social realities of surviving as a lower-income family in America. And like Will & Grace before it, Roseanne organically, even comically, depicted familial political divides by portraying Roseanne Conner as a Trump voter and her sister Jackie as a Hillary Clinton supporter.

After series lead Roseanne Barr tweeted a racist slur about Valerie Jarrett, a senior aide to President Barack Obama, ABC Entertainment president Channing Dungey terminated the series on May 29, 2018, following its renewal for an 11th season on the network. Then, the following month, ABC announced it was ordering 10 episodes of a spin-off about the family titled The Conners, which regenerated by killing off the character of Roseanne, ending just last year after seven seasons on the air. If anything, the show’s unlikely staying power proves that if a show sticks to its DNA, it can outlast even the messiest of scandals.

The four-episode return of Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel’s mother-daughter dramedy was rightfully docked for its extended, gratuitous Stars Hollow musical involving Tony Award-winning performers (and ex-spouses) Sutton Foster and Christian Borle. But a bit of superfluous song-and-dance naturally feels right at home for Glee, and even Girls—an encore version of Marnie singing Kanye West’s “Stronger” would reach cringeworthy new depths.

The pregnancy revelation that ends Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life should have kicked the revival off, not concluded its story. Instead, A Year in the Life emphasizes just how little Rory and Lorelei have grown in the years since Gilmore Girls ended, only to leave the revival’s most compelling leap forward for its final moments—and totally unresolved. After a decade, the bait-and-switch still burns, which speaks to the divisive, and enduring, nature of TV returns themselves. As for the next chapters of Glee and Girls, may the writers’ rooms hear our post-election pleas.

The Law & Order franchise has seen a lot of guest stars over its three-decade run. Many actors appeared before they made it big, while others simply wanted to come play amidst their success. Even now, during Season 28 (which is airing on the 2026 TV schedule), the guest stars are bringing the power. This includes New York Knicks point guard and NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, who guest-starred in Thursday’s episode. However, it's worth noting that his cameo was extra special because it was a full-circle moment for both Mariska Hargitay and Knicks fans.

It’s no secret that Hargitay is a major Knicks fan. While she’s a SoCal girl, she’s been living in the Big Apple for decades because of SVU, and she's proven time and time again that she's committed to the hometown team. I mean, she ran to Game 4 of the NBA Finals after finishing a Broadway show, and has been seen freaking out on the sidelines.

As for Brunson, his dream of appearing on SVU finally came true, as he played Detective Madison (evidently named after MSG) and helped Benson with a case. During his scene, he made some fun references that sound like something an NBA champ would say, too, and I loved every second:

My goal was give 110%, things worked out.

This appearance on Law & Order: SVU has been a long time coming. On top of Hargitay being a major Knicks fan, Brunson has previously shared his love for the long-running NBC drama. Over the summer after the Knicks won it all, he even admitted he wanted to “try and get on SVU.”

Plus, he and Hargitay have been friends for a while; he even showed up to her Broadway play, so it really was all just a matter of time until his cameo happened. And I’m so happy it finally worked out.

"Blew a 0.25 and started yelling at me" –– Detective Madison aka Jalen Brunson to Mariska Hargitay on Law & Order SVU With cameo from Rick Brunson https://t.co/18bDIOQxtpNovember 6, 2026

Along with this being a full-circle moment for fans of the Knicks and Hargitay, Brunson's appearance on SVU marks his second time dabbling in acting. In September, he hosted the Season 53 premiere of Saturday Night Live, and he did a very good job. He’s one of many athletes who have been on the variety sketch show, and I wouldn’t be surprised if this wasn’t his last time at Studio 8H. Even though basketball is his focus, especially after becoming an NBA champ, who knows where his SNL and SVU appearances could lead him.

Considering Brunson and Hargitay are so close -- so much so that the actress is the only celebrity who gets to hug the NBA star -- I feel like this appearance would have eventually happened with or without the Knicks winning the NBA Finals. However, Brunson manifesting this cameo after winning probably helped it get fast-tracked.

Since the point guard plays a fellow detective who knows Benson, I feel like it's possible for us to see Detective Madison again. But now that the basketball season is in full swing, it might be hard to get another appearance in there any time soon. However, I'm so overjoyed that they squeezed in this one appearance in the wake of the Knicks winning the championship.

New episodes of Law & Order: SVU air on Thursdays at 9 p.m. ET on NBC, streaming the next day with a Peacock subscription.

#3640. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle Are Moving Again

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have reportedly found a new home in the Cotswolds, less than three months after their return to the United Kingdom. But anyone who thinks they’ve bought a new home will be disappointed. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who had been staying at the residence of a wealthy entrepreneur friend since August 26, have reportedly left the main house on the property to move into another residence located within the same estate, according to Daily Mail journalist Richard Eden. “They were living in the main house,” a person close to the entrepreneur told the British newspaper. “They have now moved to a property on the estate.” The move reportedly took place before Harry and Meghan left for a vacation abroad with their children.

Since the couple returned to the United Kingdom, their search for a new home in Britain has been a hotly debated topic, especially in light of their disagreements with the royal family and security concerns. The mystery surrounding their residence has fueled speculation and various theories. Where would the Sussexes choose to settle? That was the question echoing everywhere on social media and in the press. For security reasons, the details of their living arrangements have always remained confidential.

As reported by the British media, the couple and their two children had been staying at a property owned by a wealthy friend, nestled in the Cotswolds countryside—an area Harry and Meghan already knew well. In 2018, the year of their wedding, they rented a prestigious farmhouse in the region for two years—a historic property with an estimated value of 4.12 million British pounds (about $5.5 million), part of the Great Tew Estate. The residence included a four-bedroom farmhouse, a barn converted into living quarters, and a separate cottage with two additional bedrooms. The property also featured extensive grounds and a heated patio. Over the years, the Cotswolds, in the English countryside, have become a retreat for numerous celebrities, including Jeremy Clarkson, David and Victoria Beckham, and Kate Moss. A few weeks ago the Duchess of Sussex was photographed at The Three Horseshoes, a quaint pub near Burford, in the company of Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi. In 2024, DeGeneres and de Rossi left the United States to move to the Cotswolds, where they live on a large estate surrounded by greenery.

The Sussexes’ housing history in the United Kingdom, however, has been quite eventful. Before leaving the United Kingdom, the couple lived at Frogmore Cottage in Windsor, a property made available to Harry and Meghan by Queen Elizabeth II. In 2023, however, the two royals left the residence. The decision came a few months after the publication of the duke’s memoir, Spare. To renovate Frogmore Cottage, approximately 2.4 million British pounds (about $3.2 million) went into transforming two existing buildings into a single-family home. The renovations were extensive: The ceiling beams and floor structures were replaced, the electrical system was redone, new gas and water lines were installed, and a soundproofing system costing approximately 50,000 British pounds (about $67,000) was reportedly put in place. Despite the significant spend, the Sussexes left the property for good after moving overseas.

Even before settling in Windsor, Harry and Meghan lived at Nottingham Cottage, within the Kensington Palace complex. It was a rather small residence that apparently hadn’t won Meghan over. In the Netflix documentary Harry & Meghan, the duchess recalled with a touch of irony that the name Kensington Palace suggested something grand, while the reality was quite different: “Kensington Palace sounds very regal, of course it does. It says ‘palace’ in the name. But Nottingham Cottage was so small!” Harry added that the house had very low ceilings and was even slightly slanted.

The new home in the Cotswolds could therefore be a practical solution for the Sussexes, at least until they figure out their plans in the United Kingdom. Meghan’s professional commitments may also take her away from England again. The duchess is expected to move temporarily to Australia next year to participate in the filming of Junior MasterChef, the cooking show she is set to cohost. Prince Harry and their two children might join her during her stay in Australia, but there’s no confirmation of that yet.

The identity of the estate’s current owner remains a mystery. He is a friend of Prince Harry’s, with whom he shares a commitment to charities that support veterans and military personnel. Apparently, the businessman would be happy to continue hosting the prince, Meghan, and their children for a long time to come. Several theories have circulated regarding the benefactor’s identity, with some speculating that he is Ian Wace, a British financier with an estimated net worth of $1.2 billion and who has long been close to Harry. He owns the Rowler Estate, a vast estate in the Cotswolds. His private life has been marked by tragedy: In 1994 he lost his first wife, Joanna, and their two young children in a car accident in Hampshire.

However, being hosted by a wealthy friend is nothing new in the Sussexes’ lives. In 2020, when they decided to step back from their royal duties and move to the United States, the couple stayed at the Beverly Hills mansion of producer and media mogul Tyler Perry. It was a Tuscan-style residence with eight bedrooms and 12 bathrooms, located within the gated community of Beverly Ridge Estates.

A few months later, in August of that same year, Harry and Meghan purchased a mansion in Montecito, California, where they settled. Surrounded by greenery, the mansion is located in a residential area frequented by some of Hollywood’s most famous stars, including Oprah Winfrey, Ariana Grande, and Brad Pitt. It is a very luxurious home that, at the time of purchase, was dubbed the Sussexes’ new palace—one the couple seems to have no intention of selling, despite their return to the United Kingdom. According to reports, the maintenance staff had continued to care for the family’s chickens.

The couple is still holding on to the California property, purchased for around $14 million, which continues to serve as one of their family homes. The estate includes a wine cellar, a movie theater, a gym, a spa, a large swimming pool, a tennis court, a wood-fired oven, a barbecue, and more than 13 and a half bathrooms.

However, this is not the only residence owned by the Sussexes. Just several years ago, Harry and Meghan purchased a home on the Portuguese coast, near the one owned by Princess Eugenie—Harry’s cousin—and her husband, Jack Brooksbank. The property is located within the CostaTerra Golf & Ocean Club, an exclusive residential complex with about 300 ocean-view villas in Melides, south of Lisbon.

Meanwhile, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are expected in Brussels on November 10 for an event dedicated to protecting children from online risks and abuse. The heart of the initiative, organized by MEP Antonio López-Istúriz White as part of a parliamentary intergroup, will be the unveiling of The Lost Screen Memorial, a video installation created in memory of children who lost their lives after falling victim to online abuse and exploitation. The installation will consist of 50 large-scale portraits of the young victims. European Parliament president Roberta Metsola is also expected to attend the ceremony.

According to reports in the British media, Harry and Meghan will deliver a joint speech on the issue—which has long been a focus of the couple’s advocacy—before participating in a discussion with international activists. Among the scheduled speakers is Sandra Spitaels, the Belgian mother of Glenn, who, in 2017, took his own life at age 15 after a nude photograph of him was circulated online.

These two developments involving the Duke and Duchess of Sussex come as Meghan’s father, Thomas Markle, is at the center of a horrific legal case. He is the subject of an investigation launched following a complaint filed by his son, Thomas Markle Jr., with the Philippine police and the FBI. The younger Thomas handed over to investigators a box containing several images and videos that allegedly depicted child sexual abuse, found among his father’s personal belongings in Cebu City, Philippines.

Another discovery reportedly took place in recent days at a storage unit that Thomas Markle allegedly rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico. The facility was reportedly inspected by local police as part of an investigative operation. Meghan’s 82-year-old father has reportedly been transferred in recent days to a facility in Florida that specializes in caring for people with dementia, according to The Sun.

His move to a care facility could now complicate the investigation, particularly the possibility of questioning Thomas Markle. His cognitive condition could make it more difficult to proceed with the investigation, especially given the protections afforded to residents of specialized facilities.

Meghan, who has had no contact with her father since 2018, has not commented on the latest developments. It had previously emerged that the duchess, who had been aware of the allegations against her father since 2018, wanted to speak out publicly. One of the agents from Royalty and Specialist Protection (RaSP)—the Scotland Yard unit responsible for the security of members of the royal family and other public figures—reportedly advised her not to speak out. The agent reportedly told her, “Leave it with us, we’ll investigate it.”

Thomas Markle was arrested in Florida on Friday on charges connected to the possession of child sexual abuse material. He has previously denied possession of such material.

Originally published by Vanity Fair Italia.

#3638. I Think One Wild Horse Nine Performance Is 100% Oscar-Worthy (And I’m Loving That Reviews Agree)

Martin McDonagh’s movie Wild Horse Nine has finally premiered on the 2026 movie schedule, and John Malkovich has firmly cemented himself as an Oscars frontrunner (at least in my mind). However, I’m not the only one saying that. Many reviews for this dark comedy highlight the actor’s performance, with some even pointing out that a trip to the Academy Awards might very well be in his future.

Much like McDonagh’s other movies, like the beloved Banshees of Inisherin, Wild Horse Nine is a tragic comedy. And much like Seven Psychopaths and In Bruges, it’s also a film full of action. In it, John Malkovich plays a CIA agent named Chris, and he's on a mission with his pal/fellow agent, Lee (Sam Rockwell), that leads them to Easter Island. Both Malkovich and Rockwell give masterful performances in this film; however, it's the Being John Malkovich star who gives a true masterclass as he plays out the deeply sad yet funny journey Chris is on.

Critics can’t help but praise the actor, either. In Brian Truitt’s review for USA Today, he specifically said Malkovich should be in this year’s Oscar race, writing:

Malkovich is known for his oddball supporting roles, so it’s a treat when he gets to really do his thing as a lead. And he makes a meal out of Chris, a guy who’s maddening for those around him, yet is also an absolute hoot to watch. As a man who becomes almost an unreliable narrator of his own story, Malkovich brings an amazing amount of depth and a wry sense of humor to the role, so good it’s put him back in the Oscar race. (Considering he’s never got a golden dude in his iconic career, Malkovich has a good chance to win, too.)

Truly, a common theme among Wild Horse Nine’s reviews is the praise for Malkovich. Calling him “magnificent, wryly funny, a bit scarily intimidating, and moving in a way that can’t easily be quantified,” Deadline’s Pete Hammond had this to say about Wild Horse Nine’s lead and his partner in crime, Sam Rockwell:

Malkovich is the perfect if unexpected casting here and it is one of those performances that after you see it is hard to imagine another actor doing as well. Rockwell may not have quite the quotable off-the-wall dialogue McDonagh has gifted Malkovich but nevertheless anchors the relationship in such ways that really makes this story work as well as it does. Both are simply superb.

While not every review mentioned the awards race, many did note that John Malkovich was doing some career-best work in Wild Horse Nine. For example, Matt Zoller Seitz gave the film 3.5 out of 4 stars, writing in his review for Roger Ebert:

The movie gives you all this, plus some of the best acting ever done by Malkovich, Rockwell and Buscemi (who’s aging into his silver-haired scene-stealing character actor phase beautifully), a characteristically daffy (though fragmented) supporting turn by Parker Posey as Lee’s ex back home, and one wickedly quotable line after another.

There are some line readings in this film that will stick with me forever. Recalling a scene where a bug crawls on Malkovich while he’s narrating memories of his life without him noticing, Consequence’s Liz Shannon Miller noted that the actor’s performance is truly “remarkable,” writing:

He’s that locked in. Touches like that highlight the remarkable nature of his mind-blowing work in the dark comedy, a performance that gives Wild Horse Nine so much of its power — a movie small in scale but mighty in its themes.

This review is also headlined to note that Malkovich will “blow your mind and break your heart.” I’d also like to add that he’ll make you laugh, and it’s how he manages to balance all of that that makes his performance so Oscar-worthy.

The CBC’s review for Wild Horse Nine notes that both Rockwell and Malkovich have “generated a wave of very credible Oscar campaign buzz.” Meanwhile, David Fear wrote that it was the Con Air actor FTW in his piece for Rolling Stone:

But this is a John Malkovich for-the-win affair. And his interpretation of Chris — sometimes cantankerous, sometimes childlike, sometimes flaky and forgetful, forever suffused with a metastasizing sense of guilt over his past misdeeds — is what makes the film draw blood even in its sillier, more surreal moments.

Now, if you look at the current predictions for the 2027 Oscars, both Variety and Gold Derby have John Malkovich listed as a top contender for Best Actor. He’s been nominated twice before in the Supporting Actor category (for Places in the Heart and In the Line of Fire); however, despite all the great work he's done, he’s never won, and he’s never been recognized for a leading role.

I think Wild Horse Nine gave him the perfect opportunity to show off all his skills as an actor, and I really, really hope it leads to him taking home the gold in 2027. It would seem the critics have a very similar feeling too.

To see if you agree, you can check out Wild Horse Nine in theaters now.
