#3547. 10 Classic TV Finales That Have Aged Like Fine Wine

It’s much easier to have an exciting TV pilot than a satisfying finale. After years of building characters, relationships, and storylines, the best TV finales deliver conclusions that honor everything that came before. Unfortunately, even some of the most beloved TV shows have stumbled at the finish line.

After six seasons of building an intricate mythology, Lost's series finale prioritized emotional closure over answering many of the island mysteries thatkept audiences invested. Meanwhile, Game of Thrones lost much of its political nuance and increasingly rushed through major storylines after moving beyond George R.R. Martin's published books, culminating in a divisive final season.

On the other hand, some finales are instant classics, like Breaking Bad, which delivered a near-perfect conclusion to Walter White's story. However, since the Breaking Bad finale isn't even old enough to drive yet, this list focuses on older shows.

For this list, "classic" refers to shows whose cultural significance has endured, rather than a specific era of television. The show's ending must have become even more impressive over time, whether through its storytelling, emotional payoff, or influence on subsequent television.

Many of these finales were groundbreaking when they aired, establishing conventions that modern television still follows. Whether they delivered long-awaited closure, subverted expectations, or redefined what a television finale could accomplish, these 10 endings have only gotten better with time.

The two-part finale of The Fugitive helped establish the modern television series finale, with its second installment becoming the most-watched television series episode in history up to that point. At the time, networks didn't fully appreciate the importance of giving audiences a proper sendoff for characters and stories they had spent years investing in.

However, The Fugitive demonstrated just how much viewers valued a satisfying conclusion. After four seasons of Dr. Richard Kimble fleeing Lieutenant Gerard while searching for the one-armed man who murdered his wife, the finale finally delivered on the show's original premise. Kimble's innocence was proven, bringing his years on the run to a definitive end.

Nearly six decades later, the Fugitive finale has only become more impressive, especially considering the many modern television shows that have struggled to deliver satisfying endings. The Fugitive proved that sometimes the perfect conclusion is simply fulfilling a show's original promise.

Q transports Captain Picard between three time periods to investigate a phenomenon threatening to erase humanity from existence in the Star Trek: The Next Generation two-part finale, "All Good Things...". The title invokes the familiar expression "All good things must come to an end," which Q himself uses during the episode.

The universally acclaimed finale brings the series full circle by revisiting its pilot, "Encounter at Farpoint," in which Q first puts humanity on trial for its barbaric nature. Seven years later, Picard must once again prove humanity's worth, this time by demonstrating its capacity to evolve beyond conventional thinking.

Series finales can be difficult to watch for many reasons, including ending badly, heartbreaking twists, or we just don't want to see the show go.

The finale also celebrates the relationships forged over seven seasons, culminating in Picard finally joining his officers' poker game. More than three decades later, "All Good Things..." has aged even better because the subsequent TNG movies never achieved the same consistent acclaim as the television series. The Next Generation finale remains one of the crew's finest adventures.

Newhart's series finale delivered one of television's most memorable final scenes: a twist revealing that the entire sitcom had been a dream experienced by Dr. Robert Hartley, Bob Newhart's character from The Bob Newhart Show. The earlier series had ended four years before Newhart premiered, making the surprise return of Hartley and his wife Emily (Suzanne Pleshette) especially memorable.

Rather than offering a conventional conclusion, the finale recontextualized eight seasons of storytelling with a single joke. Beyond its comedic brilliance, the twist offered an unexpectedly touching reunion of two beloved characters, letting audiences revisit the familiar warmth of Newhart's earlier sitcom.

Seeing Bob and Emily together again gave the finale a sense of nostalgia and emotional closure that its absurd premise might otherwise have lacked. Frequently parodied in the decades since, Newhart demonstrated that a sitcom could deliver a satisfying farewell by completely subverting expectations.

Cheers' three-part series finale was a massive television event, with NBC estimating that nearly 40% of the U.S. population watched it live. More than 500 people, including several cast members, gathered in Boston to celebrate the beloved sitcom's conclusion.

Despite its enormous audience, critics were divided. While some praised its emotional sendoff, others felt the renewed Sam and Diane romance leaned too heavily into melodrama, overshadowing the ensemble humor that made Cheers so beloved. However, the finale's emotional restraint has become easier to appreciate over time.

Sam's realization that the bar is his true love reinforces the importance of the makeshift family he has built there. The final moments, with Sam alone in the bar after everyone leaves, are bittersweet rather than tragic. Life goes on, but "One for the Road" was the perfect nightcap.

"Family Meeting," the series finale of The Shield, received widespread acclaim for bringing its morally complex story to a satisfying conclusion. The finale pays off the events of the pilot, in which corrupt detective Vic Mackey murders undercover officer Terry Crowley to prevent him from exposing the Strike Team's crimes.

Seven seasons later, Vic once again sacrifices a fellow officer to protect himself. He escapes punishment, but loses his family, his colleagues, and the power that once defined him. Instead of prison, he finds himself trapped behind a desk, a fitting punishment for a man who thrived on bending the rules.

What makes the ending so satisfying is that Vic's downfall feels both inevitable and entirely self-inflicted. He survives by betraying everything he once claimed to value, making his victory indistinguishable from defeat. The final moments leave just enough ambiguity about whether Vic can ever truly change.

The Mary Tyler Moore Show series finale reinforces the groundbreaking premise established in its pilot: a woman choosing independence over marriage. Instead of ending with a wedding, the show delivers a surprising twist when nearly the entire WJM newsroom is fired.

Mary realizes that, although she's losing her job, the relationships she's built have given her something more lasting. Her final speech, in which she acknowledges that her coworkers have become her family, reinforces the show's message that fulfillment doesn't have to come from traditional relationships.

The emotional group hug, which hilariously turns into a collective shuffle toward a box of tissues, balances humor and heart perfectly. The Emmy-winning episode is one of the best sitcom endings of all time. Although its unconventional ending is less revolutionary today, that's partly a testament to The Mary Tyler Moore Show​​​​​​'s influence: what once subverted television conventions has become the standard for meaningful sitcom farewells.

The two-part Cowboy Bebop finale, "The Real Folk Blues," has aged beautifully because it refuses to give its protagonist a conventional happy ending. Instead, Spike Spiegel's tragic fate reinforces the anime's central argument: the past cannot be changed, but refusing to move beyond it can destroy the possibility of a future.

After a tragic loss, Spike chooses to confront his enemy rather than embrace the found family he has built aboard the Bebop. This decision makes the finale heartbreaking because Spike has finally found somewhere to belong, but cannot recognize it as a reason to keep living.

Flawless anime finales often tie themes and character arcs together, delivering an earned and unforgettable finale that's true to the story’s vision

His ambiguous final moments, accompanied by Yoko Kanno's haunting music and Cowboy Bebop's closing message, "You're gonna carry that weight," leave audiences contemplating the cost of his inability to let go. The poorly received 2021 Netflix live-action remake only reinforced how difficult the original's distinctive blend of action, melancholy, and existential storytelling is to recreate.

Few sitcom finales have delivered as devastating a tonal shift as Blackadder Goes Forth's "Goodbyeee." Throughout its four series, Blackadder reinvented itself in different historical periods, but the World War I-set final series culminated in something far more devastating than audiences expected from the historical sitcom.

After spending the series desperately trying to avoid combat, Blackadder makes one last unsuccessful attempt to escape the trenches by pretending to be insane. Even the usually oblivious Baldrick recognizes the hopelessness of their situation, while the relentlessly cheerful George admits he's frightened.

When the order finally comes to advance, Blackadder's sarcastic defenses disappear, replaced by quiet resignation. The soldiers charge into no man's land, and the image fades into a peaceful field of poppies. Rather than abandoning its comedic identity, the finale reveals the humanity beneath its satire, unexpectedly giving audiences one of the bleakest endings in TV history.

The two-and-a-half-hour M*A*S*H finale, "Goodbye, Farewell and Amen," was one of the most highly anticipated television events in history. CBS charged $450,000 for a 30-second commercial, more than NBC charged during that year's Super Bowl. As of 2026, M*A*S*H remains the most-watched episode of a TV show in U.S. history.

The episode balances the psychological toll of combat with the bittersweet relief of finally going home. After tearful goodbyes, the 4077th goes its separate ways. As Hawkeye departs by helicopter, he discovers B.J.'s farewell message spelled out in stones, a final reminder of the friendships that made an unbearable war survivable.

Six Feet Under’s finale "Everyone's Waiting" is widely considered one of the greatest series endings in television history. The episode opens unlike any other in the HBO drama: not with a death, but with a birth, immediately signaling its shift from confronting mortality to celebrating life.

As the Fisher family begins moving forward after Nate's death, their grief gradually gives way to hope and the possibility of new beginnings. This culminates in Claire's departure from Los Angeles, accompanied by an extraordinary montage that reveals how each major character eventually dies.

Rather than undermining their hopeful futures, these glimpses of mortality make every moment of happiness more meaningful. Few finales have achieved such complete narrative and emotional closure while so perfectly encapsulating their show's central themes. More than two decades later, "Everyone's Waiting" remains the gold standard for TV endings.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

The set includes Aragorn, Arwen, Gimli, Lurtz, and a Nazgûl. Putting Arwen and a Ringwraith in the same box makes it tempting to stage a little flight to the Ford, while Lurtz gives Aragorn somebody to square off against at Amon Hen. Each figure comes in its own box with a display base and roughly two to four points of articulation. Lurtz also has movable eyeballs, so if you put him next to Gimli, you can make sure he’s looking down at him.

Asmus has made a realistic sixth-scale Aragorn before, complete with Mortensen’s likeness and a detailed costume. The QBitz figure gets away with doing much less. The dark cloak and layered ranger gear put him squarely in his Strider days, and that scowl could belong to the guy who just found out Merry and Pippin lit a fire on Weathertop. Of all the versions of Aragorn you could shrink to four inches, the one who spends half of Fellowship trying to keep four hobbits out of trouble is an especially good fit.

Asmus lists the five figures together, with a $20 nonrefundable deposit and a limit of three sets per customer. The company says it will email buyers when the set is ready so they can pay the remaining balance. The preorder page currently does not list a shipping date.

#3541. Every Highly Anticipated Fantasy Book Adaptation Trapped in Development Hell

Book adaptations are a special kind of joy and pain for readers, but that's especially true when you spend years waiting for them to come to fruition. Though terrible adaptations can be devastating for fans, big fantasy hits like Game of Thrones prove they can work both for existing fans and newcomers alike. But though many series have been picked up in the wake of some major hits, several of the most anticipated fantasy book adaptations have really stalled.

The last few years have seen a few major, long-awaited series officially canceled. In 2023, Netflix ditched its Shadow of Bones adaptation after just two seasons. The planned Six of Crows follow-up got scrapped altogether. But while those cancellations are tragic for fans, many fantasy readers are stuck wondering whether their book adaptations will ever cross the finish line.

Some books are optioned for film or TV adaptations, but linger in limbo. So-called "development hell" can happen to projects for many reasons. For fantasy books in particular, the cost-benefit analysis for CGI budgets can take ages. That means series that seem like obvious wins, including ACOTAR, can spend years in pre-production before they ever hit our screens.

Brandon Sanderson's Mistborn series has seen quite a few false starts in the adaptation realm over the years. The wildly popular fantasy series has been optioned a few times, but prior attempts to bring the series to the screen fell through. However, hope for a Mistborn adaptation is far from dead.

Earlier this year, Apple TV snagged the rights for the entire Cosmere universe. Better yet, they asked Sanderson himself to write the script. The author confirmed that he's got a good feeling about this latest adaptation attempt. Even so, the fact that we've been waiting for so long to see an adaptation come to life lands this project solidly in the development hell category.

Given how popular ACOTAR is in the book world, an adaptation seems like an obvious move. Yet Hulu let the rights lapse without ever bringing the series to fruition, leading to a devastating cancellation. But it's not all bad news for fans. Earlier this year, Maas confirmed she's not given up on getting her series made into a movie or TV series. She is working to find another studio willing to take on the project.

The trouble with ACOTAR is that, while the books are popular, they'll require a good bit of CGI to bring to life. The series is set primarily in a fantasy realm, and the big budget attached ultimately scared Hulu away. Though there could be a Game of Thrones in it for whoever steps up to the plate next, more recent fumbles like Shadow and Bone likely have studios scared to spend on such high-budget projects with no guarantee of success.

You can purchase A Court of Thorns and Roses here.

Brandon Mull's Fablehaven series is a modern fantasy classic by many rights, with over 3.5 million copies sold. And yet, despite a few studios poking at the project over the years, it's yet to get a single adaptation. That could finally be about to change, however.

A recent Fablehaven crowdfunding project on Backerkit soared past full funding and then some. In theory, that means Angel Studios is finally going to make a Fablehaven adaptation a reality. Since the campaign wrapped in April, the company has provided sporadic updates on social media. But it will likely be some time yet before the movie comes to fruition.

Lionsgate Studio optioned the rights to adapt Patrick Rothfuss's Kingkiller Chronicle series over 10 years ago. Since then, we've seen a few false starts, including a Showtime prequel series with Lin-Manuel Miranda. After that series fell through, Lionsgate has resumed its search for a network or streaming service to pick it up.

In part, the hesitation to pull the trigger on The Kingkiller Chronicle could be related to its unfinished status. Though wildly popular, the series hasn't yet released its final book. Showtime, and other studios Lionsgate tries to approach, may be worried about repeating the old Game of Thrones ​​​​​​problem. As such, we might be waiting a while before this project gains any traction.

You can purchase The Name of the Wind here.

In theory, the next several years could deliver on some massive fantasy adaptations. There are quite a few big series that have announced TV or movie versions on the way. However, many have stalled out, with few updates since their initial adaptations. There's always hope that they're moving forward behind the scenes, as none of these fantasy adaptations have been officially canceled, either.

As many writers know, books are often optioned without ever getting adapted. This step just means that someone has paid for exclusive rights to adapt a book, if they decide to. It doesn't mean they plan to move forward so much as they see enough promise in a series that they want to avoid letting anyone else get ahold of it. That means these series are even less likely to happen than those that have been formally announced.

#3539. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3536. Inside 'The Rings of Power's Darkest Season Yet — and Gandalf's Quest To Save Middle-earth

The cast and creators break down the show's most personal storyline yet for Tolkien's most iconic wizard.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is about to enter uncharted territory — but that's exactly why creators J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay are excited.

When Prime Video's blockbuster fantasy series returns for Season 3, it won't be resuming right where viewers last left off in the Second Age, with Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and the Elves announcing their fight against Sauron (Charlie Vickers) and his encroaching army of Orcs. Instead, the story jumps ahead by five years, to a point when the era known as the War of the Elves and Sauron is already in full swing. The new Dark Lord's influence is slowly but steadily skulking across Middle-earth, with only a few regions still untouched by the encroaching evil. While Payne and McKay admit the show's time jump represents a "jolt of energy" in moving the story forward, they also hope it'll serve as a different opportunity for any potential viewers who haven't tuned in to the show before.

"It is, in some ways, starting afresh," Payne admits. "All you really need to know is: these guys are at war." With Sauron taking even more diabolical steps to recruit potential allies (more on that later), the number of individuals who are not just willing but able to withstand his invasion seems at an all-time low. Yet eagle-eyed fans may have noticed one character in particular who's already being positioned to face off against Middle-earth's greatest threat — sometimes literally in the marketing itself.

"We've been slowly building this character from a tabula rasa into one of the most iconic heroes in Tolkien's legendarium," Payne says. It's an evolution that's taken years of work on and offscreen, likely testing some fans' patience in the process, but Season 3 represents a big step forward in a much greater odyssey for Middle-earth's most renowned wizard. Below, Payne, McKay, director Sanaa Hamri, and actors Daniel Weyman, Ciarán Hinds, and Zubin Varla break down what to expect from The Rings of Power's most powerful and personal storyline yet for Gandalf.

Given where The Rings of Power's story picks up, "darkness" feels like a perfectly succinct description — and not just because the third season begins with a snapshot of the evil creeping across Middle-earth. While the series has never shied away from the murkier corners of Tolkien's world, Payne and McKay wanted Season 3's narrative shift into distinctly heavier territory to feel as earned as any other aspect of the show.

"It is a darker season, but I don't know that we approached it self-consciously wanting to be darker so much as trying to take seriously a world that is at war, where the heroes are losing, where evil is ascendant," McKay explains. "Evil in Tolkien is not simple. It is complex. It corrupts good. That means you're going to have characters who fall to evil forever, and it means you're going to have characters who can die. By taking that seriously and treating it authentically, it's going to lend itself to a darker season."

While those life-and-death stakes are rising for every character who's been swept up in this war, nowhere do they feel more apparent than in the company of Sauron, who has finally embraced his truest self after two seasons of deception and manipulation. That unmasking set the tone for everything across Season 3, including behind-the-scenes details big and small.

"I really allow the story and what the characters are going through to influence the direction and the tonality," Hamri, who returns to direct several episodes this season, explains. "If you look at the season, Sauron, for the first time, is now embodying the Dark Lord. First, he was Halbrand, then he was an Elf. Now, he's in his full glory. He's no longer hiding."

The Dark Lord, now capable of replicating Celebrimbor's (Charles Edwards) greatest triumph in Season 2 to the best of his own abilities, has some powerful rings to "hand out," as Payne puts it — and sends missives out across Middle-earth with the promise of awarding them to those men he deems most deserving. If that invitation sounds too good to be true, that's because it is; Sauron's rings of power are in short supply, and anyone who puts themselves in a position to claim one may have to pay a deadly price.

Lest you think that this means Season 3 is all doom and gloom, however, The Rings of Power's creators emphasize that the War of the Elves and Sauron only makes up one piece of the larger puzzle. This is an epic fantasy world, after all, but one that has always maintained a delicate balance between good and evil.

"Middle-earth is a place where people are dealing in life and death. The stakes are real. That's one of the reasons we were excited about adapting this material," McKay says. "It's got real dramatic stakes to it, but it's also balanced with wonder and awe and beauty and humor. The way we approach making that stew with the right ingredients every season is we just try to commit to every one of these stories and the characters, and really try to treat them seriously.'"

"It's really easy for things to get too grim, especially in a world in which there's war and death around every corner," Payne adds. "There’s got to be something that’s going to bring you back to the light."

Enter: The Rings of Power's worst-kept secret. If you've been watching the show from the beginning, the reveal that "The Stranger," who first crash-lands on Middle-earth in a flaming meteor, is actually Gandalf likely didn't land as any great twist. Now, after two seasons and 16 episodes, the secret is officially out, but if you ask Weyman, the entire ride to date has been one big gift of a role, with much of his journey off-screen paralleling the path his character has taken.

"I started with nothing; the character started with nothing," Weyman admits, referencing his time in New Zealand during production on The Rings of Power's first season — in which The Stranger finds his footing in Middle-earth, so to speak, with the help of some nomadic precursors to the Hobbits, known as Harfoots. "In some ways, I was mirroring the journey of The Stranger, and that meant that, as I came to play different scenes with different communities, or understand different things that he had to learn, they were amassing in my version of The Stranger; they were layering his character as I went."

Since filming happened mostly in chronological order, by the time Season 2's finale rolled around — otherwise known as the moment when The Stranger finally has a revelation about his true name — Weyman says he didn't feel any added pressure or weight he wasn't prepared to take on, regardless of any actors who preceded him in the role. "When the showrunners said, 'You're going to say, 'They're going to call me Gandalf, aren’t they?' which was spine-tingling and wonderful, at that moment, I felt, 'All they're doing is labeling a character who I've already created.'"

It's understandable, then, that Weyman goes on to describe his time filming The Rings of Power Season 3 in only one word: fun. On a broader level, though, he explains that his approach to performance had to change, simply by virtue of the fact that the character he was playing had transformed too.

"It was really interesting how different filming as Gandalf was from filming as The Stranger, both on set and off-set. How I carried myself as an actor was different because Gandalf, in this season, has arrived; his feet are firmly wizard-on-the-floor. I think he understands the connections to the gods up above and the earth and nature below," Weyman says. "He's understood, through his relationship with Tom Bombadil, his purpose and what he's trying to achieve, and that means that he has a lighter touch. Not everything is so dreadfully, immediately, importantly terrifying to him. Whereas The Stranger may have been very reactionary and just feeling like he's got to solve everything straight away, Gandalf understands he won't be able to control or solve certain things, and that's part of the journey. Being okay with that really changed how I played him and how I was on set."

The showrunners and cast break down some of the biggest moments from Season 2's first three episodes.

Within that mindset of grounded acceptance came the addition of what Weyman describes as another "important artifact" on Gandalf's journey. It's an element that has already been revealed in promotional material leading up to the season's premiere, but this particular gift, courtesy of Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear) himself, is merely the latest in a series of items Gandalf has collected that hold personal meaning for him.

"The staff we see in Season 2 has been picked out of a fallen tree out of the awful thing that the Dark Wizard has done to the Stoors and moved by Nori from this broken tree onto [Gandalf's] path, effectively. I don't know how many people picked that up when they watched it, but the fact that that has come through her hands is monumentally important." Similarly, Weyman explains, Gandalf's new wizard's hat is significant in more than one sense.

"Not only is it a part of Tom with him, which is really important, but also it's got a completely massive practical use. It's part of his armor. He goes outside; he hasn't put it on yet, but when he's out there, the sun starts to beat down on his head, and he remembers Season 2, and what an awful journey it was across this desert with Nori and Poppy, and how near to the end they all got. He suddenly realizes he's got this bit of armor in his hand. He puts it on his head, and it's protecting him from this incredible power that the sun brings."

Finding the right hat for Gandalf was a "Goldilocks" process in and of itself, according to Payne, who credits The Rings of Power costume designer Libby Dempster with leading the charge after rounds of narrowing down their options. "That one is too big. That one is too small. That one is too curly. The color looks too dark, too light, too blue, not blue enough." Even once the perfect fit was chosen, Season 3 became an opportunity to pay homage to both Tolkien's epic source material and Peter Jackson's original trilogy, with Weyman's Gandalf strikingly backlit by the very sun he's stepped out into, hat officially donned.

"It's almost like an album cover," Hamri admits. "When I was editing it, and I presented it to the showrunners, it just felt like the right moment." One particular shot, which features Gandalf giving a subtle, self-acknowledging look almost directly to the audience, is the same one that made it into the finished product. "We never changed a frame," McKay declares. "From the first time we saw it, we were like, 'Well, that will be in the first trailer,' and then the first trailer that Amazon marketing showed us had the version of it in there. You just sit back and enjoy the ride when you have a moment like that."

Yet one particularly iconic piece of headgear, or even a powerful staff kept close at hand, isn't going to be enough to singlehandedly defeat Sauron and his forces — and this is where Gandalf's storyline this season simultaneously pivots to a deeper exploration of his mythological origins while keeping the stakes intimately personal.

"In the Third Age, there's a moment when he's confronting a Balrog, and he says, 'I am a servant of the Secret Fire,'" Payne notes — which, in Tolkien's legendarium, is another name for the power of Eru Ilúvatar, the God of Middle-earth. In Season 3, Gandalf is not only directly confronted by his divine origins, but is personally tasked with a mission of salvation, rather than destruction.

"We're told that the Istari are forbidden from meeting power with power — fighting fire with fire. Their role is actually to speak to the hearts of the people in Middle-earth and to try to inspire others to find their own courage and their own strength to be able to fight against the evil, to come together as unlikely allies," Payne says. "We wanted to start telling that story. What was it that started Gandalf on that path to understand that, 'My purpose, as an Istari, isn't to cast fireballs, but to inspire hearts'?"

While Gandalf isn't quite as removed from the rest of the story as he was at the beginning of the series, Weyman confirms that he can't link up with other potential allies immediately, which forces him to plan from behind enemy lines while other characters make bigger political moves. "What he's trusting in this season is the idea of: do what you can in the present with the beings you interact with. Do all you can. It means trusting yourself. It means trusting your instincts."

Remember when we mentioned that there are still some holdouts in Middle-earth that have been able to withstand Sauron's skulking influence? One of them — Rivendell — likely comes as no surprise, given the Elves' firm resolution to battle the Dark Lord at any cost, while the other is being ruled by a different sort of evil, one who shares a personal history with Gandalf himself.

The Dark Wizard, first introduced in The Rings of Power's second season as an Istari who has yet to reveal his own true name, has kept most of his cards pretty close to the vest, but Hinds says he considered his return to the role, his second reprisal in a major fantasy franchise, a "huge adventure." Despite establishing his home base in Rhûn, a vastly uncharted desert region in the east, and having several robed cultists sworn to his cause, the Dark Wizard presents, in Hinds' words, as "a rather solitary figure."

"He's not quite Nobby no-mates, but apart from his acolytes, there's no real contact with him. He's a strategist, and we don't know exactly what his strategy is, and that's what I'm playing in this season."

Instead of digging his heels in as a form of resistance, however, the Dark Wizard makes his own chess move against Sauron — sending one of his cursed servants, known as Khamûl the Easterling, as a messenger to uncover exactly what's going on in Mordor. If that name sounds familiar, that's because he's one of only two named Nazgûls in Tolkien's writings — which is originally all Varla had to go on when he was approached to play the character after providing some general voice work on Season 2.

Once Khamûl and Sauron are in each other's orbit, you can probably guess what happens next, but Varla confirms that the carrot being dangled through a ring of power, after a lifetime under the Dark Wizard's thumb, ultimately proves too tantalizing to resist. "Khamûl is somebody who'd already been subjugated. His people were already not what they once were. He is already, when we first meet him, enslaved, as generations before him had been enslaved, by Wizards. The land is no longer his. He has an axe to grind. He has something that he wants back; he just does not have the power at that particular point to get it back. What Sauron offers them is the power to take back what is rightfully theirs."

Naturally, when Khamûl returns, he's a very different being than the one who first departed Rhûn, much to the Dark Wizard's dismay — but Hinds asserts that his character simply considers it a countermove in the ongoing game he and Sauron are playing, rather than a sign of defeat that forces him to kneel. "They're testing each other out in a way. The Dark Wizard has never been challenged like this before, and suddenly this force doesn't surrender to him." Although Khamûl may be newly equipped to confront his long-time oppressor, Varla adds that his power has a secret and more nefarious source. "There's something coursing through Khamûl that he is yet not in control of, and doesn't understand. That’s Sauron coursing through him. That's a new world that he's yet to come to grips with."

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

With the Dark Wizard caught between a rock and a hard place, Gandalf — who's quietly been looking for a way to dismantle his fellow Istari's white-knuckled grip on Rhûn — finds himself at a critical crossroads. With strength in numbers now essential for not just confronting but ultimately defeating Sauron, does Gandalf have the power to sway an old friend away from the darkness and back to the light? It's a more meditative question that leads to no shortage of action for these characters, but Payne admits that the writers didn't want to start from a place of magical combat, which felt like a predictable retread of what viewers had seen before.

"As we were really thinking about Gandalf's larger series arc, that he has to speak to the hearts of people in Middle-earth, we thought, 'What an impossible mountain that is to climb, someone who has gone as far toward the dark side as the Dark Wizard has gone. What if Gandalf has to figure out a way to try to turn him?' It's such an impossible situation to put your character in that it felt delicious to us as dramatists to try. Knowing Gandalf has to try to figure out how to help his erstwhile tardy colleague find redemption felt like the right story for us to tell this season."

Weyman points out that the long history between the two characters, which has yet to be fully illustrated onscreen, alongside the subtle proof of the friendship that once existed between them, gives Gandalf's biggest emotional duty this season a bittersweet significance. "The Dark Wizard seems sad. He was sad in Season 2 when he uttered the words, 'old friend.' How could we be friends if you behave like this? If we were friends, is there any of that friendship still alive? It is very difficult to believe that Gandalf ever got on board with a friendship that was around suppressing and controlling and subjugating. It's very difficult to believe that. So, if we don't believe that, that means there must have been something in the friendship that was joyous and light and loving and charitable."

Hinds turns equally philosophical when asked about the journey the Dark Wizard and Gandalf embark on together in Season 3, which touches on greater themes of betrayal, sacrifice, and the question of whether salvation is possible. "Power in the hands of good people can be so beneficial, who have intelligence and understanding. We know that, and yet, what does seem mad is that whoever has the power, you don’t trust them because they get warped along the way. That idea of allying yourself for the good against the dark has gone on forever, but it's something that I think we all connect with, no matter how fantastical it can be. There's something at the heart of all this which is true to the journey of the people on our planet."

For Weyman, it's taken six years to reach Gandalf's biggest evolution yet — and for the fans eagerly awaiting The Rings of Power's return, the wait has likely felt just as long. Fortunately, Season 3 is finally poised to bring the story's most powerful opposing forces together. With the fate of Middle-earth hanging in the balance, the cost may very well be a bigger sacrifice, as Gandalf himself notes in the season's latest and most foreboding trailer, but the creators' hope is that the show's latest and darkest chapter yet has been well worth the wait.

"We have asked an enormous amount of audiences in having Gandalf’s journey be a slow burn that led him all the way off the map, seemingly, from all the other stories," McKay admits. "But hopefully, as you watch this season, what you realize is that his destiny, even though it was leading him one way geographically, was cosmically, emotionally leading him straight to Sauron."

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 premieres November 11 on Prime Video.

#3533. James Wan’s Paranormal Activity Reboot Release Delay Officially Restores Franchise Tradition

James Wan's Paranormal Activity film has officially been delayed, but this shakeup means it will restore a long-time tradition for the horror franchise.

Wan is no stranger to the horror genre, having created The Conjuring franchise, directed Saw and Insidious, and produced Annabelle, The Curse of La Llorona, M3GAN, Lee Cronin's The Mummy and Backrooms, among many others. Now he's joining the Paranormal Activity franchise as a producer of the eighth film.

Variety reports that the next Paranormal Activity movie will be released on October 22, 2027, instead of May 21, a delay of five months. Aside from the 2014 spinoff Paranormal Activity: The Marked Ones, every sequel in the main series of films has been released in October, which means this change by Paramount ensures that a Halloween release schedule continues.

Joining Wan as producers on the reboot are Jason Blum, Oren Peli, Steven Schneider, Michael Clear, Judson Scott and Alayna Glasthal, with Ian Tuason serving as director. The filmmaker previously helmed several short films and made his feature-length directorial debut with the 2025 horror flick Undertone.

Tuason is following in the footsteps of previous Paranormal Activity directors Oren Peli, Tod Williams, Henry Joost, Ariel Schulman, Christopher Landon and Gregory Plotkin. The franchise began in 2007; since then it has collectively grossed around $900 million at the box office.

Its critical reception has been much more mixed, to say the least. The very first Paranormal Activity is the only film to earn a Certified Fresh score on Rotten Tomatoes, where it's currently at 82%. After that, the ratings have precipitously dropped, with Paranormal Activity 3 receiving the next-highest score at 68% and Paranormal Activity: The Ghost Dimension having the lowest score at 16%.

Across eight films so far, Paranormal Activity has leaned on the found footage format to tell supernatural stories of families who get haunted and murdered by a demon. The most recent installment was the reboot Paranormal Activity: Next of Kin, which was released on Paramount+ instead of in theaters because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

#3532. Apple now explicitly bans employees from using confidential information in prediction markets

Apple has updated its insider trading policy to explicitly prohibit employees from using confidential information to bet on prediction markets. Here are the details.

Following yesterday’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings report, Apple today published its fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, which is a mandatory annual filing with the SEC that provides a detailed look at the company’s finances, business, and risks.

Among the documents included in the filing is an updated version of Apple’s insider trading policy.

Until last year, Apple’s insider trading policy, filed with the SEC as Exhibit 19.1, included the following prohibitions:

However, the updated policy includes a new prohibition:

No Trading in Prediction Markets Based on Confidential Information. Do not participate in “prediction markets” or similar platforms to wager, bet, trade, buy or sell contracts based on the outcome of future events, or otherwise enter into event contracts, when such activity involves the use of Apple Confidential Information (as defined in Apple’s Business Conduct Policy) about Apple or any other company (including Apple suppliers, manufacturers, vendors or customers, such as cellular network carriers or other business partners) obtained in connection with your work at Apple. You must also not tip Apple Confidential Information to others who may participate in such markets. Apple Confidential Information includes, but is not limited to, material nonpublic information. This prohibition applies whether or not the activity constitutes insider trading or securities trading under applicable laws.

While much of this may seem obvious, how insider trading rules apply to prediction markets has been something of a gray area, to put it mildly. And while major prediciton markets explicitly ban the practice in their terms of service, enforcement remains a challenge.

In Apple’s case, the new language explicitly extends restrictions beyond traditional securities trading, making it clear that employees cannot use confidential information to place bets on prediction markets, even when those transactions don’t qualify as insider trading under applicable laws.

You can read Apple’s full 2026 Form 10-K on its Investor Relations page.

#3529. macOS 27.3 adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look

Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details.

Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and new tools for third-party developers.

Among the smaller changes coming to the Mac is a welcome improvement to Quick Look. As of macOS 27.3 beta 1, .md files are rendered with proper formatting directly in Quick Look, rather than displaying their raw Markdown syntax.

Apple has been expanding Markdown support across its platforms, including the ability to import and export Markdown files in Notes. Markdown has also become increasingly important with the rise of AI agents, which use .md files to store instructions, context, and other information.

In fact, as Federico Viticci noted today on X, Apple’s new Siri AI app skills feature also uses Markdown-based SKILL.md files, allowing developers to provide instructions that help Siri perform complex tasks within their apps.

What a journey for Markdown, @gruber The new Siri AI developer framework now officially uses skills, with specific Markdown guidance for SKILL .md agent files https://t.co/koi8K541le pic.twitter.com/TF72JJZRXc

For the uninitiated, Markdown is a simple text formatting syntax created by John Gruber in 2004, and has since become widely used for writing documentation, publishing content online (including this very post), and, more recently, providing instructions to AI agents.

Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for web writers. Markdown allows you to write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format, then convert it to structurally valid HTML.

In practice, this means you can create headings, bold text, lists, and links using just a few simple characters. And, starting with macOS 27.3, you’ll be able to preview the results directly in Quick Look, without having to open the file in a separate app.

To learn more about Markdown, follow this link.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3522. Paramount's Next Big Fantasy Franchise Officially Arrives in 10 Weeks

2027 is shaping up to be another big year for fantasy adaptations. Not even two full months in, Netflix will release Greta Gerwig's much-anticipated Narnia: The Magician's Nephew in theaters on February 12, marking the first movie from C.S. Lewis' literary world to reach the silver screen in over 15 years. On December 17, 2027, meanwhile, Andy Serkis will bring viewers back to Middle-earth with The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum, complete with Ian McKellen, Kate Winslet, Lee Pace, and Elijah Wood reprising their roles from Peter Jackson's trilogies. It's not just books getting the big-screen treatment either. Sony's The Legend of Zelda will take to the fields of Hyrule on April 30, headlined by Benjamin Evan Ainsworth and Bo Bragason in the iconic roles of Link and Zelda.

For Paramount's fantasy ambitions, however, the charge will be led by Children of Blood and Bone. Based on Tomi Adeyemi's breakout hit fantasy novel of the same name, the film will introduce a new audience to the Kingdom of Orïsha and the young woman, Zélie Adebola, who seeks to restore its magic. Thuso Mbedu will play Zélie on her journey as she wields the powers granted to her by the gods themselves to strike back at the oppressive regime ruling her people and take back what was so violently ripped from them. Along the way, she'll make some powerful allies too, with the daughter and son of the king joining the fight against the monarchy to forge a better future. A full seven years after Fox 2000 initially optioned the YA book, its release is finally close at hand.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

As of writing, only ten weeks remain until the ambitious adaptation hits theaters on January 15. Gina Prince-Bythewood, who last worked with Mbedu in the Viola Davis-led epic, The Woman King, in 2022, took the reins of Children of Blood and Bone as both director and co-writer alongside Adeyemi. Davis is also part of the star-studded cast, which prominently features The Acolyte alum Amandla Stenberg as Princess Amari and F1's Damson Idris as Prince Inan, alongside Tosin Cole, Cynthia Erivo, Lashana Lynch, Zackary Momoh, Richard Mofe-Damijo, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Regina King, and Idris Elba.

While there's been plenty of anticipation to see how the New York Times bestselling West African mythology-inspired epic translates to film, one person who's not particularly excited for the film is the author herself. Adeyemi is credited as the co-writer of the screenplay, but openly distanced herself from the project over the summer, describing a "painful" falling out in a series of posts on social media. "I have not seen the film, and I will not watch it," she added, also writing that she ultimately left because she couldn't "continue being hurt and attacked behind the scenes." Much of her frustration was specifically directed at Stenberg, who had previously indicated the author herself wanted her involved in the adaptation. Exact details of what transpired are unknown, but it has sown some uncertainty about the production and how it will ultimately treat Adeyemi's source material.

Children of Blood and Bone launches in theaters on January 15. Stay tuned here at Collider for more updates as it draws near.

#3521. Bill Cosby Accuser Wants Arrest Warrant Issued Over Unpaid $59 Million Judgment

Bill Cosby could find himself back in handcuffs ... because one of his sexual assault accusers wants a judge to issue a warrant for his arrest, claiming he's been blowing off court orders related to the massive judgment he owes her ... TMZ has learned.

According to court documents, obtained by TMZ, Donna Motsinger is asking a judge to hold the disgraced comedian in contempt ... telling the court Cosby's been refusing to cooperate after a jury ordered him to pay her a whopping $59.25 million in her civil sexual assault case.

Donna claims Cosby hasn't paid a single penny of the judgment ... and has ignored demands to turn over information about his finances, including his bank accounts, income and assets.

In fact, she says a judge ordered Cosby on October 9 to cough up the financial information and pay $1,560 in sanctions within 10 days ... but he allegedly did neither.

Now, Donna wants Cosby dragged into court to answer for allegedly blowing off the judge ... and she's asking for a warrant for his arrest if he doesn't show up.

And she's not stopping there ... Donna is also seeking up to $1,000 in fines and five days behind bars for each alleged violation, plus $3,284 in attorney's fees and costs. She's even asking for Cosby to be jailed until he complies with the court's orders if he's found in contempt and continues refusing.

As TMZ previously reported ... a jury found Cosby liable in March after Donna accused him of drugging and sexually assaulting her in 1972. She was awarded $19.25 million in damages, plus another $40 million in punitive damages.

Cosby later tried to get the verdict tossed and secure a new trial ... but in May, a judge rejected his efforts. He appealed the rulings to a higher court, which remains pending.

A hearing on Donna's latest request is scheduled for January.

#3519. 7 Neo-Westerns Better Than Marshals

Taylor Sheridan's Marshals is a great neo-Western series, but there are seven other neo-Westerns that blow it out of the water. The Yellowstone spinoff series Marshals is one of the biggest success stories the neo-Western genre has ever seen. Marshals season 2 is now the most-watched show on cable, it's steadily upping the stakes and tension of Kayce Dutton's story, and it's going bigger and better than ever before.

Even with the almost unprecedented success Marshals has enjoyed, the show has a few shortcomings. Most noticeably, Marshals has the worst Rotten Tomatoes score of any Taylor Sheridan show. Critics and some viewers have made it fairly clear that Marshals is not the best television show ever made. Marshals does, however, have its fair share of advantages, from its excellent cast to its connections to Yellowstone.

Still, Marshals isn't a great representation of all that the neo-Western genre has to offer. Some of the best Western shows of the past decade have been set in the modern day, and they've far surpassed Marshals in terms of quality. If you've been watching Marshals and want something that scratches that same itch but is a bit more enjoyable to watch, these seven shows are certainly worth checking out.

It should be no surprise that Marshals' parent show, Yellowstone, is a better neo-Western. The most famous neo-Western ever made, Yellowstone follows the Dutton family as they protect their titular Montana ranch from those who wish to take it. The show delves into family drama, action, politics, and every other part of life in the West. Bolstered by Taylor Sheridan's fantastic writing and dialog, Yellowstone is easily one of the best neo-Western shows out there.

Marshals' ties to Yellowstone certainly helped it become a breakout hit, but they also expose why the original is so much better than the spinoff. Yellowstone is gritty, complicated, and filled with morally gray characters doing heinous things in service of protecting their ranch. Marshals simply doesn't have as much bite, and it's "case of the week" format keeps it from telling an overarching story as big and bold as Yellowstone's central plot.

Dark Winds, created by George R.R. Martin and Robert Redford, is arguably the greatest neo-Western of the 2020s, and it easily surpasses Marshals. Dark Winds follows three members of the Navajo Tribal Police — Joe Leaphorn, Jim Chee, and Bernadette Manuelito — as they solve crimes that border on supernatural. Though the show takes place in the 1970s, it's modern enough in both technology and themes to be considered a neo-Western.

Yellowstone may be the most popular neo-Western show out there, but Game of Thrones creator George R.R. Martin made an even better Western series.

Like Marshals, Dark Winds is also a police procedural. Dark Winds, however, handles its mysteries a lot better. Each season presents a new case with ties to Navajo folklore, and each of those cases is dripping with thematic weight, suspenseful twists, and brilliant pacing. On top of that, Dark Winds has one of the most talented casts on television in general. Dark Winds and Marshals have a lot in common, but the former executes on those similarities much more efficiently than the latter.

Another Western police procedural, Longmire, also has Marshals beat. Longmire follows Sheriff Walt Longmire of Abseroka County, Wyoming, as he solves crime using common sense and country knowledge instead of expensive crime scene analysis. The show mainly follows a "case of the week" format, but Walt also has to contend with overarching problems from land developers, the nearby Cheyenne reservation and its casino, and solve the murder of his wife.

Though it doesn't quite rise to the level of Dark Winds, Longmire is a close second in terms of neo-Western police procedurals. Walt and his deputies are interesting and complex characters, and the mysteries they're confronted with are real head-scratchers that invite the audience to play along. It's a more traditional mystery show than Marshals, but that's actually an advantage for Longmire.

Though supernatural horror and neo-Westerns don't typically mix well, Preacher proves that blend can be executed masterfully. Preacher follows Jesse Custer, a priest, who teams up with his murderous ex-girlfriend and a vampire to literally battle the forces of evil with guns and bullets. Part Buffy the Vampire Slayer, part Ash vs Evil Dead, Preacher is nothing if not distinct.

Preacher couldn't be more different from Marshals, which is one of the reasons it's better. Marshals isn't a terribly original show. Not only is it a spinoff of Yellowstone, but other shows have focused on U.S. marshals, tense family dynamics, and grieving widowers. There is no other show that's quite like Preacher. It's unapologetically weird and leans fully into its oddities. The result is a series that takes big risks that often pay off and feel completely unique. Marshals often feels like it has no identity, and that's never the case for Preacher.

Timothy Olyphant and Walton Goggins' Justified is arguably the greatest neo-Western show ever made. Justified follows Raylan Givens, a U.S. Marshal, and Boyd Crowder, a career criminal. As Raylan dismantles criminal enterprises throughout Kentucky, Boyd serves as his nemesis and occasional reluctant ally. Justified is basically the protoytpical neo-Western: it has action, a Southern setting, themes about the fight between good and evil, and one of the best hero/villain dynamics in TV history.

Justified also has quite a bit of overlap with Marshals, given their shared focus on U.S. marshals. That overlap also makes it abundantly clear that Justified is the better show. Its episodic and season-long mysteries and criminal conspiracies are more complex and intriguing, its characters are more colorful and nuanced, and its writing is top-notch. This isn't really a slight against Marshals; Justified is just one of the best neo-Westerns out there.

Westerns and science fiction mix quite well, as evidenced by space Westerns like The Mandalorian and Firefly. Outer Range, however, chose to lean further into neo-Western elements than sci-fi ones, and it paid off in dividends. Outer Range is a mystery box show that sees Royal Abbott struggling to keep his Wyoming ranch afloat when a mysterious black void appears on the property, though that's just the start of his problems.

Outer Range is a bit difficult to talk about, as unraveling the mystery of the void is much of its fun. Without delving into spoilers, however, it's safe to say that Outer Range is one of the most inventive, surprising, and mysterious neo-Western shows on this list. Unfortunately, it was canceled after just two seasons. The seasons it did get to premiere, however, feature fantastic acting, casting, and a twisty plot that can keep anyone on the edge of their seat.

Another blend of Western and sci-fi elements comes from Wynonna Earp, and it once again proves that blend can be exceptional if done right. Wynonna Earp follows the titular Wynonna, a direct descendant of Wyatt Earp, the legendary real-life lawman who was present at the Shootout at the O.K. Corral. Wynonna inherits Wyatt's mythical revolvers and a mission to return the ghostly spirits of Old West outlaws to Hell.

Wynonna Earp may not be a traditional neo-Western, but it more than makes up for that by providing everything you could want out of one. Wynonna is a great protagonist with a lot of character, the supernatural story lends itself perfectly to classic neo-Western themes surrounding the past and generational trauma, and it's packed to the gills with great action scenes. Marshals may be getting its flowers now, but Wynonna Earp is still worth revisiting.

#3517. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.
