#3515. 3 Great Thriller Books You Can Start and Finish This Weekend (November 7-8)

Few things are better than reading a great book that's also quick to reach its ending. A long, detailed, winding book has its own benefits and charms, and some of the all-time works in literary history are well beyond 1000 pages. Yet, sometimes, all you want is a short and sweet story that takes only a couple of days to finish.

If you're on the hunt for a great thriller story that you can start on a Saturday morning and end on a Sunday night, you're in luck, because there are more than a few great options. From certified classics of the genre to newer stories full of mystery and danger, these are three great thriller books that you can finish over a weekend. So sit back, find yourself a comfortable spot, and get ready to spend some time with these gripping stories.

Let's begin with a proper classic, shall we? Agatha Christie is the legendary author behind some of literature's greatest and most timeless mystery novels, from Murder on the Orient Express to The Murder of Roger Ackroyd. However, none of her novels is as celebrated, well-known, or re-readable as And Then There Were None. The plot centers on ten strangers invited to a secluded island by a mysterious host. There, each one is accused of committing a previous murder, and when each one starts dying, the survivors realize the killer is among them.

The word "classic" is overused, but it truly applies here. And Then There Were None is a foundational entry in the thriller, crime, and mystery genres, the quintessential whodunit, and a pillar of 20th-century literature, not to mention the best-selling mystery novel of all time. More to the point, it's an incredible piece of narrative, endlessly compelling and incredibly entertaining, to the point where its 272 pages go by in a flash. Christie is among history's best writers, and her ability to craft addictive mysteries is on full display here; her web of complexities makes it genuinely hard to anticipate the twists and the killer's identity. A true page-turner, And Then There Were None is so good that you might even finish it in one day.

Moving on to the 21st century, we have one of the most disturbing and unforgettable thriller books ever written. It's even more impressive to consider it was Kanae Minato's debut novel. Confessions follows middle school teacher Yuko Moriguchi, who is grieving the death of her four-year-old daughter, Manami, in what was ruled an accident. Yuko soon realizes three of her students are behind Manami's death and decides to carry out a sinister revenge plot, delivering one final lesson to her students before quitting.

Confessions is among the most chilling thrillers of the 21st century. Minato opts for a straightforward approach that is equal parts gripping and stomach-churning, especially in Yuko's now-iconic confession. The book adopts a truly neutral stance on the nature of justice and morality; nearly every character walks a line between "good" and "evil," not only the student killers but also those around them and Yuko herself. Through the two student characters and the teacher willing to descend into the depths of darkness to avenge her daughter, Minato questions the dynamic between teenagers and adults, and showcases how neglect and generational misunderstanding can lead to tragedy.

Lastly, we have another relatively new book that is on its way to becoming a modern classic. Set in Lagos, Nigeria, My Sister, the Serial Killer tells the story of Korede, a young nurse whose sister, Ayoola, constantly kills her boyfriends, claiming it was self-defense. Thus, Korede must help clean the crime scenes and dispose of the bodies. Things change when Ayoola sets her sights on Tade, a handsome doctor with whom Korede has been in love for a long time. Now, Korede must grapple not only with her jealousy and hurt but with the fear that Ayoola will kill Tade next.

My Sister, the Serial Killer is one of the best thrillers you can read. At only 240 pages, the story moves along at a brisk pace, arriving at a harrowing conclusion that is both profoundly bleak and in tone with the overall story. Author Oyinkan Braithwaite focuses on themes of family loyalty, duty, and the deep sense of responsibility so many feel towards their family members, even when their choices are destructive and actively dangerous. Yet, My Sister, the Serial Killer is also quite funny, with a macabre, dark humor that makes a decidedly sinister story that much more addictive.

#3505. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

#3499. With iOS 27.3, Apple will start checking iCloud public links for ‘harmful content’

iOS 27.3 adds lots of new iPhone features, and it also makes a change to how public iCloud links work with the aim of preventing harmful content from being shared. Here are the details.

This week Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta, which adds Siri AI improvements, new Safari features, the all-new Apple Health app, and more.

Per a newly published support document on Apple’s website, iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and more also include a key change to how iCloud public links work.

Apple currently provides two main options when sharing photos, files, and more via iCloud. You can share with ‘People you choose’ or create a public link that works for ‘Anyone with the link.’

Starting with iOS 27.3 and companion updates, the ‘Anyone with the link’ option will start being checked by Apple for harmful content.

When you share content that’s stored in iCloud, such as a photo in iCloud Photos or a file in iCloud Drive, you can choose to Share a Link or Send a Copy of the item. If you choose Share a Link, you can either share the item with “People you choose” — only people you invite or approve — or with “Anyone with the link,” which makes it accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple. Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content.

If Apple flags the content you’re sharing as harmful, the support doc says it “reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time.”

I’m okay with Apple doing this. HOWEVER, they should publish at least rough guidelines on what they will consider “harmful”.

Saying nothing more than “harmful” leaves way too much open to arbitrary interpretation.

For anyone trying to upload harmful content, the company may “take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement.”

As outlined above, choosing the ‘Anyone with the link’ option has always made it accessible to “anyone who has the link, including Apple.” That’s because it’s a public link.

What’s changing now, though, is that Apple says it will begin checking those public links for harmful content.

Do you use iCloud public links? What’s your take on this change? Let us know in the comments.

#3495. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3486. Security Bite: The record $6.3B Binance heist started with a fake Homebrew install on Mac

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Last week, news broke that hackers had stolen $6.3 billion from wallets on Binance, the most popular cryptocurrency exchange in the world. The company was able to freeze about nearly $3 billion of it, but the attack quickly made headlines, and rightfully so, as the largest financial heist in human history.

At the time, I suspected, along with security researcher Christopher Lopez and plenty of others, that this could have very well started on a Mac. As Lopez pointed out, the $1.5 billion Bybit heist last year also began on a developer’s Mac. On top of that, Macs are hugely popular among DevOps engineers and crypto folks, and they’ve been on the receiving end of a steady stream of malware and social engineering campaigns over the past few years.

I can now say any suspicions that this heist originated on Mac were right. I’m still in a state of shock. Dazed not by the amount stolen, but how the said hackers did so using the same ol’ social engineering tricks they’ve been using for years. No sophisticated multi-milllion dollar underground zero-day here.

Yesterday, Binance published a more detailed breakdown of the attack. The company never actually says “Mac,” but the malware it published targeted /opt/homebrew, which is where Homebrew lives on Apple silicon Macs. In other words, this was almost certainly an M-series MacBook.

The attack basically transpired in two steps.

According to Binance, in June this year, a DevOps engineer working on Wallet searched for an AI coding tool and downloaded a malicious clone of the Homebrew installer in Google Search. Binance claims it caught it early and stopped any damage. However, what it didn’t know was that it allowed the attackers to learn which employees worked on its wallets. This was phase 1.

Fast forward a few months to September, a different engineer who, you guessed it, worked on wallets for Binance, was lured into a fake job interview. As these sort of social engineering attacks normally go, they told to run a coding “assignment” on their work computer. This was not caught by Binance security, and on October 29, the world learned that hackers (now widely speculated as North Korean hackers) walked off with billions.

Of course, most of what we know so far comes directly from Binance, so if you’re looking for more details on exactly how this happened, you’ll likely be left empty-handed.

It’s important to note here though, none of these two attack vectors are new. Back in early 2025, I wrote about fake Homebrew ads at the top of Google Search pushing Atomic Stealer to Mac users. Binance only says the engineer found his installer through “a search engine.” Of course, I can’t confirm it was a sponsored ad, but if history tells us anything…

This is a rather uncomfortable situation for Apple to be in. The largest financial heist in history happen on Mac last week, though to be fair, there’s no security feature that can stop a developer from running a script he wants to run.

Sure, the Terminal paste warnings introduced in macOS 26.4 could have helped here. But realistically, if someone’s convinced they’re doing a coding test for a job they really want, a warning pop-up probably isn’t going to stop them.

I’m having Christopher Lopez (@L0Psec) a professional macOS reverse engineer back on the Security Bite Podcast this week to talk about the Binance situation with me. Follow the show so you don’t miss that.

#3485. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: eight to 10 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

#3484. Remix Albums Are Helping Pop Acts Live in the Moment Longer — And Feel Less Alone

When Underscores joined Porter Robinson on the Smile! : D tour in 2025, she noticed something unusual about his set. “Perfect Pinterest Garden,” a showy deep cut from the musician’s third studio album, didn’t sound quite the same.

“You’re playing it one semitone down,” she told him. Underscores would know — it’s her favorite song on the maximalist pop record released in 2024, and she has an affinity for any song played in its original key. When Robinson made the adjustment during his next soundcheck, he saw her beaming.

That exact level of perception and specificity made Underscores a perfect recruit for Smile! : D Plus+, an ambitious remix album that dismantles and reassembles Smile! : D with appearances from 16 artists. During his hunt for collaborators, Robinson looked for people who bleed music. “They just care, and they’re actually deeply passionate, and the details matter,” he tells Rolling Stone. “The things that people might not even be able to hear — those things matter to them.” Underscores put her expertise to work on an explosive new version of “Perfect Pinterest Garden” alongside fellow pop disrupter Ninajirachi.

“[Underscores] and Nina just brought all of the life back into it,” Robinson says. “The added verses, the re-recorded parts, the way it’s kind of turned into an electro dance remix — it’s just brimming with life now.”

Remix albums have been common practice for decades, but as audience attention spans dwindle and artists look for creative partnerships that are more personal than transactional, the pop remix album has an even greater function. Smile! : D Plus+ follows recent releases from PinkPantheress, Zara Larsson, Charli XCX, and more in pouring a little more love and a little more life into community and collaboration.

After the Smile! : D tour ended, Robinson passed his time playing DJ sets that turned up the energy on some of his most contemplative songs. Smile! : D is his most cerebral release, a meticulous assessment of parasocial fan culture and external pressure that turns inwards. “I realized that a lot of people in the world had this notion of me that was just a totally incomplete piece of the picture, and that was scary to me,” Robinson says. He communicates so much on the record, but figured if anyone didn’t get it the first time, Smile! : D Plus+ might break through to them. “I care so much more about my pop songs than about high energy DJing,” he says. “I like both, but I care about my songs the very most.”  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Robinson gave his Smile! : D Plus+ guests their pick of the original track list. “I didn’t want to force it,” he says. “I didn’t want to make them do a song that they weren’t feeling.” This applied even to songs already claimed by other artists — it’s why there are four new versions of “Cheerleader” and three of “Is There Really No Happiness?”, including one from Frost Children. The electronic duo of Angel and Lulu Prost are the only featured guests who also appeared on the original album. But where “Mona Lisa” takes a classic pop approach to affection, their distortion of the melancholic “Is There Really No Happiness?” amplifies progressive trance gate elements Robinson hinted at on his own. He’s always felt the song never got its proper due.

“I always thought if you stripped the instrumental and just heard the vocal, you would hear it as this beautiful EDM melody,” says Lulu. “I wanted to pick one that wasn’t already pretty hype and turn it into something a lot more crazy.” Angel started by crafting a melody out of vocal chops from Robinson’s acapella recording. Frost Children’s dance music DNA took over from there. The final version runs for seven minutes, nearly twice as long as the original. “You could play this entire thing in a set and it takes you on a journey you get lost in,” Lulu adds. “Old trance songs are like 10 minutes long, and it’s just looping, and then finally a euphoric melody comes in.” Related Content Turnstile Raise Over $250,000 for Charity at Massive Free Washington D.C. Show Chappell Roan Concludes Benefit Shows With Surprise Duets Featuring PinkPantheress, Lola Young See Charli XCX and Chappell Roan Perform 'Boom Clap' in Los Angeles Zara Larsson Transforms Into a Fairy, a Mermaid, and More in ‘Blue Moon’ Video

Frost Children attempted to trim their edit down, but found themselves wondering, “What’s the point of making a remix if you’re gonna compromise everything again, anyways?” These days, the duo have an influx of remix requests coming in. Signing on for Smile! : D Plus+ was an obvious yes — Lulu got a tattoo for Robinson’s album Worlds when they were 17 and attempted to hide it from him while they worked together. “In high school, that era of Porter’s music meant a lot to us and still does,” they say. “I was too embarrassed to show him.” When Lulu finally revealed it, Robinson admitted he knew the whole time.

“Within this last year, we’ve seen the rise of so many artists who I think themselves would say that they grew up on my albums,” Robinson says. Being able to call on those artists now positions him as something of a mentor, but he’s also a fan. “Ninajirachi, Underscores, Frost Children, they’re forging their own path,” he adds. “They have a machete and they’re cutting through the wilderness and discovering something new.” The admiration is mutual, even as they become collaborators and friends. “All of us are gagged that we’re talking to him,” Angel says.

Robinson liked the Frost Children version of “Is There Really No Happiness?”, but suggested they change just one chord to create a more euphoric feeling. It made all the difference. Before, Frost Children were never really sure how to make notes without overstepping. It’s something they’ll carry into their own work. Compromise is an essential component of collaboration — like when producer Margo XS had to sacrifice some of the ambient dreamscape French musician Malibu created for “Saturn’s Return” from Zara Larsson’s expansive remix album Midnight Sun: Girl’s Trip.

“It was definitely too sleepy to get everybody, including the label, on board to put on a mainstream pop remix album,” Margo says. She restructured the song with songwriter Helena Gao, but saved Malibu’s mystique for the end, which brought an airy feel to its introspection. Margo and Larsson went into Girl’s Trip imagining what it would be like to make Midnight Sun over again, this time with the creative familiarity they’ve fortified in the past year. In that time, the album marked a true, long-awaited breakout for Larsson. Girl’s Trip allowed her to let that moment breathe, and share it with 13 other artists, including Margo, JT, Tyla, Robyn, and more.

Larsson initially planned to release a traditional deluxe edition of Midnight Sun, with a few remixes and new songs. But Margo and MNEK, who also worked on the record, “felt a lot of freedom and excitement by being able to take these stems and flip them on their head.” It’s how they ended up with an elevated R&B version of “Blue Moon” featuring Kehlani. Robinson felt similarly revitalized by stripping back to the bare bones. “Some of the remixes are speaking to the DNA that was in the song from the very beginning in a roundabout way,” he says. “Easier to Love You,” for example, started as a Eurodance song inspired by Gigi D’Agostino’s “I’ll Fly Away With You,” but ended up as a sensitive guitar ballad. Smile! : D Plus+ brought that original sound back through Dutch hardstyle DJ Vertile.

Margo describes the art of the remix album as community building, and sees it as a response to years of indifferent pop features that seemed to serve little creative purpose beyond boosting streams. “OK, you got this feature — but the production doesn’t change over it. It feels phoned in. It feels like you were just trying to maybe combine audiences and get some more love from the algorithm gods,” she says. “People got a bit fatigued from that way of working.” A remix album, on the other hand, “makes it feel very intentional in these collaborations and allows people’s identities to really flourish, and then continue to create a community around a certain style of music.”

The creation of Girl’s Trip overlapped with the release of Fancy Some More?, a remix album from PinkPantheress that revamped her mixtape Fancy That? “We were definitely inspired by her willingness to platform alternative producers and alternative voices on a pop record,” Margo says. The project features everyone from JADE and Anitta to Basement Jaxx and Kaytranada. “It just made it feel like the sky was the limit in terms of what we could do in terms of production and features.” Like, Smile! : D Plus+, Fancy Some More? includes multiple configurations from different artists. There’s a version of “Stateside” with Kylie Minogue, another with Bladee, another with Groove Armada, and of course, the breakout remix featuring a killer verse from Larsson.

After trading aesthetics in the “Stateside” video, PinkPantheress and Larsson appear together again on the Girl’s Trip version of “Midnight Sun.” An innovative producer herself, PinkPantheress and her collaborator Count Baldor worked closely with Margo to shape the song. “I really relate to how committed she is to doing a sonic aesthetic across a whole record,” Margo says. Charli XCX was in the same headspace when she released Brat and It’s Completely Different but Also Still Brat in 2024. “There’s still so many different versions of that song that could be made using a tiny element of the production from the original, or a tiny reference to a lyrical concept, or a literal lyric,” she said at the time. “It can all be deconstructed and put back together again. Why not? Why just be like, ‘It’s the album, and it’s done?’”

The possibilities are endless, especially when it comes down to locking down features. For Girl’s Trip, Larsson reached out to potential collaborators via DMs, shifting her approach depending on whether she already had an existing relationship with them. Sometimes MNEK made the connection. Margo can’t quite remember which route led to Shakira featuring on “Eurosummer,” but does recall the craziness of that particular yes. “We gotta figure this out,” she thought. “We gotta make this a bop.” It wasn’t the only version they made. There’s a “Eurosummer” remix with Romanian dance-pop stars Alexandra Stan and Inna sitting on a computer somewhere. “I know that has been very wanted by the internet, and there were a lot of rumors going around about it,” Margo says. “It does exist. That’s all I can say.”

Robinson’s process was far more free-flowing in comparison. He primarily reached out to friends and people he thought would be cool to spotlight, like the indie-pop singer EJEAN who he found through a twist of fate (read: Instagram Reels, in an incredibly rare instance, he says). “I would love to hear your version of ‘Year of the Cup’ because I think you would make the most heartwrenching version of this,” Robinson said in a message to EJEAN.

“Year of the Cup” is not really the kind of song you can flip. The original ballad samples a Lil Wayne interview from 2009 in a way that is both disjointed and completely enchanting. “It’s almost impossible to make a dance remix of it,” Robinson says. EJEAN covered it instead. Their stripped back acoustic version is the standout moment on Smile! : D Plus+.

It struck Robinson to process someone else singing words that hold so much weight to him. “When I heard them say ‘something’s in the air like vanilla,’ or these experiences where I know specifically where my two feet were in the world when those moments happened in my real life,” he says, “it gave me this twisted up feeling inside. It was like, ‘I wonder what that means to them.’” Even beyond lyrics, the sheer tone of a voice can communicate emotion so differently. Turnstile showed as much with Never Enough: Versions, a 22-track cover project with a host of guests including Hayley Williams, Elton John, and A. G. Cook. “You put everything into making an album,” Robinson says. “Anything that you can do to refresh it and remind people of its importance and remind people of what it means to you, and extend its lifespan culturally — I think there’s good reasons to do that.”

There’s a certain trust and vulnerability required to let another artist reconfigure songs born from such specific experiences and perspectives. Sometimes, doubt gets in the way. Robinson considered reaching out to Jane Remover to participate in Smile! : D Plus+ through the rapper-producer’s EDM side project, Leroy. There were threads of influence and connection there, but they hadn’t properly met before, so he decided against it. “I was too shy to ask,” he says. “I should have just asked.” He would have also loved to hear something from Smile! : D reimagined by a K-pop artist, like KiiiKiii or Aespa, similar to how PinkPantheress recruited Seventeen for “Illegal.”  Trending Stories A Jesuit Priest Explains How He Facilitated Bob Dylan’s Meeting With the Pope Appeals Court Says Lawsuit Over ‘The Pitt’ Can Proceed, Cites ‘Numerous’ Similarities to ‘ER’ Adam Lambert on His Future With Queen, New Music, and Why the Show Must Go On Pink Floyd Mark ‘Animals’ 50th Anniversary With Reissue Featuring Unreleased Music

These crossovers are as exciting for the artists as they are for the audience. They offer something new without completely compromising the original listeners fell for, while also potentially expanding their palette. “It’s a non-algorithmic, non-AI way of finding new things you like, and you’ll never find the end of things that you like,” says Angel. The special moments created on these projects — whether something as explosive as “Stateside,” or Lorde and Charli XCX working it out on the “Girl, So Confusing” remix, or Robinson pouring back into a lineage of his own influence — are the product of true connection.

“It’s so amazing for me to be able to hold hands with those people and the respect is so mutual,” Robinson says. “And doing it as a way of celebrating the album, it’s a win-win for everybody.”
